speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in bringing this resolution before the house I might refer to what happened last session. When the supplementary estimates were submitted, three or four days before prorogation, several hon. members took part in the discussion and it will be remembered that later the item was withdrawn, and I stated that the matter would be taken up next session. The reason I gave for withdrawing the item was that judging
i
from what appeared in the press and from the speeches in the house the matter had not been sufficiently studied, and I thought with a closer study of the question a better understanding could be reached. Now I am bringing the matter forward again in the shape of a bill which will be founded on this resolution. Its object is to provide for payment to the men taken back after the Winnipeg strike of 1919 of the salary they would have received had they re-entered the service in the class equivalent to the one they were in when dismissed.
It is not my intention to go into the merits or demerits of what happened at the time of the strike, but merely to relate what took place afterwards. On July 7, 1919, a special act was passed authorizing the Civil Service Commission to appoint to the permanent staff any person employed to replace anyone who went out on strike, and in January, 1920, the government agreed to an arrangement whereby employees who had gone out on strike would be re-employed, provided: First, that they had the approval of the governor in council; secondly, that they gave satisfactory assurance that a repetition of the offence would not occur; thirdly, that they passed the civil service examination; and in the fourth place, that they should begin anew in the service. The age limit was waived in their favour.
Now these ninety-six men who were taken on after the strike and reinstated as the agreement here states were demoted to lower positions; that is to say, they came in at the bottom of the ladder or as postal helpers to work their way up. That is what they were supposed to do. But when they did return to employment they were engaged in the same advanced class they had occupied in the service before the strike, although they weie paid the wages of employees of a lower grade. By way of comparison, although these figures may not be quite exact, I may put it this way in order to show what I mean. A postal clerk drawing a salary of S125 or $135 a month came back into the service as a postal helper at $85; he did the work of a postal clerk who would receive $125 but he himself received a remuneration of $85 only, or $90 as the case might be. There was that spread 'between the two.
On my tour to the coast in 1927 I stopped off at Winnipeg for three days, and this matter was brought to my attention. I went into it fully, and met a committee composed of some twenty-five or thirty persons representing all classes of postal workers in the city of Winnipeg. That committee was composed of men who had gone out on strike and had been taken back; of men who had replaced the
2250	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Veniot
strikers-there were some six hundred in all- and were working in the service; as well as of those who had not gone out on strike but had continued to work in the service. I met this committee representing these different classes of those concerned in the question, and they were all unanimous that those who had been token back, the ninety-six, should be paid the salaries which they earned. I would point out that if the intention was to punish those men by demoting them they should have been demoted not only as respects the amount of salary they received but, as well in the class or kind of work which they were to do. I have always believed in the principle that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and if these men were brought back and engaged in work of a higher class they should have been paid for that class of work; they should not have been demoted in the matter of salary alone.
After studying the situation very carefully and looking into all phases of it, without however inquiring into the pros and cons of the strike, or what may have brought aibout the strike, I submitted to the government that in my opinion these men for several reasons should receive the pay contemplated in section 1, the only section, of the bill to be brought down. As I stated before, I felt that they were worthy of their hire. I felt that other participants in the strike, those who had gone out from the service of the railways, industrial concerns and so forth having been taken back on the same conditions as previously, it would not be fair that the employees in the postal service should alone be signalled out for this demotion. That was one of the reasons on which I based my recommendation to the government, and it has been accepted. I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the house discussing the resolution; when the bill is before the committee we shall have an opportunity to go more fully into the merits of the question. Let me observe this, however. I read in one of the newspapers this statement:	"These men are in receipt
of larger salaries than they had at the time they went out.'' If that is so then there is nothing to pay them; it will not be necessary to put into operation this provision of the bill relating to those who went out, as regards any who may have reached after a few years the position wherein they would receive such salary as was paid them before the strike took place. Let me point out further that in this bill there is nothing which will give a preference in the way of seniority over the men who remained in the service or over those who were taken in to replace the strikers.

nothing to give these men a preference, in the way of seniority or classification, over the men who were taken in to replace the four or five hundred who were not taken back. When the resolution is in committee I shall ask to have it amended by the omission of these words:
And to make provision whereby certain former employees not now in the said service shall he eligible for reappointment as vacancies occur.
At the time this resolution was prepared I was not aware that there was an order in council which met that very condition. Having been made aware of it, and having obtained a copy of the order in council, I did not deem it necessary to go further than the first clause of the resolution in order to meet the conditions as I found them in Winnipeg. On January 7, 1920, an order in council was passed which reads:
Many evidences have reached the Department of Labour from ex-postal employees that they now recognize they participated unwisely in the sympathetic strike in western Canada last May, and that they sincerely regret the action they then took. The gravity of their offence against the state being now realized, the government has given consideration to the possibility of removing the bar to their application through the Civil Service Commission for re-employment in the public service, and His Excellency the Governor in Council is disposed to exercise clemency so far as reasonably consistent with necessary discipline.
Ex-postal employees may therefore be considered as eligible to be appointed to positions in the civil service for which they make application as vacancies occur, and to which, in the opinion of the commission, they are justly entitled under the regulations, subject to the following conditions:
Ex-postal workers must not be re-employed in the civil service without the approval in each ease of His Excellency the Governor in Council;
Inasmuch as a number of those affected have been a long time in the public service, and are now past the age limit fixed for new employees entering the service, it will be permissible for the commission to appoint them notwithstanding the age requirements.
The words which I wish to omit from the present resolution refer to the age limit.
In every ease before being reappointed satisfactory assurance must be obtained that a repetition of the offence will not occur.
This is order in council P.C. No. 1152, containing the report of the committee of the Privy Council, and approved by the Governor General on June 4, 1920.

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
There is nothing much more for me to say except to endeavour to correct a wrong impression which seems to have spread in certain quarters. The Montreal Gazette of April 8, 1929, contained this statement:
These men were dismissed from the service, and for some reason, which no one has ever been able successfully to explain or defend, were reinstated.
This order in council explains why these men were reinstated, and I merely draw attention to that statement in order to keep the record straight. A further reference was made to this matter, which I think should be corrected. The Gazette stated:
The Postmaster General failed to secure the passage of his bill; the measure -went through the House of Commons-to the discredit of that body, but it never left the Senate. That was Mr. Veniot's opportunity to do some learning.
Everyone knows no bill was introduced and no bill went to the senate last year; consequently this statement is without foundation.
I do not refer to it in a critical way but simply wish to keep the record clear.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mir. Speaker, the resolution
now before this house involves questions which have been fruitful sources of much unfortunate and painful discussion. I do not think it advisable to canvass the whole situation as we did last year; it is sufficient for my purposes to direct attention to the fact that a number of postal employees left the service of the crown under such circumstances as dislocated the public service and rendered it impossible for mail to be delivered in the city of Winnipeg. Later these men were offered the opportunity to go back to work but, not having availed themselves of that opportunity for reinstatement, they were later re-employed to the number of 96 on certain definite terms and conditions which constitute the contract between them and the state. Those conditions are contained in an order in council and are four in number. As the Postmaster General has stated, that order in council provided first that all who desired to re-enter the service should pass an examination before they were employed; secondly, that the age limit should be no bar to their re-employment as new employees; thirdly that they should be re-employed subject to
approval by the governor in council in each case and lastly that they should commence as new employees in the service.
That there was an unfortunate condition in Winnipeg in 1919 goes without saying. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) last year thought the observations which were made by myself were rather stronger than the facts warranted, and not having been in Winnipeg at the time of the strike I shall content myself for the moment by reading an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 8 of this year. The Free Press was a daily newspaper at the time of this occurrence. The proprietors endeavoured to publish it as such during the strike and I take it that they had a clear appreciation and understanding of the situation which developed in that city during the progress of events. The following is the editorial, headed "The Vote for the Postal Workers" which appears in that newspaper:
It is regrettable that the Dominion government did not profit by its experience last year to the extent of declining to resubmit to parliament the vote for the Winnipeg postal strikers, which they found it advisable last year to withdraw. This matter cannot be considered without reopening the whole question of the Winnipeg strike of 1919. This is something which considerations of prudence and public welfare should suggest leaving alone; for the passage of time ^ has not in the least led to any adjustment in the -points of view of those who have disagreed as to the original, motives and purposes of the strike. Last year, in a brief but bitter debate which followed the submission of the vote to the house, Mr. Bennett said the strike was, in the minds of its promoters, a consciously revolutionary movement intended to subvert the government of the country and he cited the findings of the court in Winnipeg to support this view: while Mr. Woodsworth took the line that it was a comparatively innocent development, the character of which "had been grossly misrepresented. This involved, of course, the necessity of representing the court cases, which followed the strike, as part of a policy of injustice. Mr. Woodsworth did not boggle at this requirement. He talked about dastardly conspiracies, travesties of justice. farcicial trials. _	_ *	.
This interchange of views illustrates what is bound to happen whenever the Winnipeg strike of 1919 comes up for discussion. All the old bitternesses revive. By an agreement entered into by common consent the issue is left alone pretty much in Winnipeg on the principle of letting sleeping dogs lie; but the Dominion government is prepared, it seems, to have the question stirred rap anew and made the subject of discussions, which are bound to be violent, in both the Commons and the Senate. Because it is not possible to deal with this business of paying back money to present members of the post office staff who went on strike in 1919 without bringing up the question of the merits of the great strike. The justice of making these payments can only be established if certain things are first established; that the Winnipeg strike was in itself right; that the postal workers did right in striking in sym-
2252	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
pathy with it; that the Dominion government of that day had no business to issue an ultimatum that the workers must return to work or lose their jobs; that the Dominion government did wrong in trying to man the post office and give the public a service; and that the men who took the strikers' positions had no claims to consideration and should have been turned into the street when, after the strike, the strikers returned and asked for their positions. Mr. Heenan, the Minister of Labour, took all these positions flatfootedly in 1926 when he made a recommendation to Mr. Veniot, the Postmaster General, which was the immediate cause of Mr. Veniot's efforts to induce the government and parliament to make these grants.
It is not surprising, however, that the Dominion government does not relish being put in the position of appearing to confirm these conclusions; and last session Mr. Veniot and Mr Thorson made an attempt, which will doubtless be repeated this year, to make it appear that there is no connection between the granting of this money to the postal workers and the question of the merits of the action of the postal workers in leaving their employment and defying the state. They failed hopelessly because the connection is explicit and undeniable. Mr. Thorson argued that the Dominion government was under no obligation to take the strikers back, but that, having done so, it should have put them back in the positions they held when they went on strike and at the same salary; he intimated that the post office sought out these workers because it required their services and took advantage of their necessities to pay them the minimum wages. This is a very inaccurate account of what happened. Within three months of the close of the strike a concerted effort was begun by the strikers to get the government to lift the embargo and enable them to apply for employment on terms which governed entrants to the service. They appealed to every available agency to intercede with the government to induce it to recede from its position that they could never re-enter the service. Among others, the Free Press was asked to use its influence with the government to this end and gladly. did so. But there was no suggestion of reinstatement to their old positions and salaries. Had this been their demand, they would not have got the support which enabled them to overcome the reluctance of the government, well known at the time, to recede from its position.
Having regard to the seriousness of their offence and to the distinct understanding upon which they re-entered the service., it cannot be said that these postal workers have been harshly used. With respect to employment, they were given a preference, subject only to prior claims of returned soldiers; the age limit, where necessary, was waived; and they were, for purposes of pensions and service, allowed to count the period of previous employment. They have been so advanced in the service that with the exception of one or two, who have been taken on within the last two or three years, they are all in receipt of larger salaries than they.had at the time they went out. The average increase is about fifty per cent. There is good ground for doubting the spontaneousness of their demand for additional payment; but naturally, being human, they joined in the movement when they were advised that if they all pulled together and IMr. Bennett.3
used their influence they might force the government to hand them over the money. The proposed vote last year was $115,000; this year it will be larger-the assumed figure is $15(h000. The division of this sum among ninety persons, even allowing for handsome deductions for "legal expenses", would be a pretty fat thing for the recipients; and it is not surprising that there is a persistent push to secure it.
The sum, large though it is. does not. of course, mean much to the Dominion treasury; but the Dominion government ought not to delude itself with the idea that the simplest thing for it to do and the one having the least dangerous consequences, is to pay the money and stop the clamour. The Dominion government cannot accede to this demand and pay over the money without thereby agreeing to the propositions, with respect to the postal strike, set forth above; and it cannot agree to these propositions without taking a responsibility which we should think it would be to its great advantage to avoid.
That is the editorial in the Free Press. I will now quote from another newspaper, The Farmer's Advocate and Home Magazine of London, of April 18, 1929, which I think publishes a western edition. The paper is entirely out of politics and its criticism of what is being done is as follows;
Politics in the Postal Service
Canadians have had reason in the past to point to our postal service as an example of successful state ownership of a great public utility. Irrespective of partisanship and political affiliations the people of Canada have expressed their pride and confidence in this department of government; but if the Postmaster General succeeds in reinstating and reimbursing the post office employees of Winnipeg who sided with the red element during the desperate strike of 1919 the Post Office Department will soon be known as a mere political cesspool.
This action to restore the strikers to the same position and status they would now enjoy had they never defied the crown nor joined the revolutionary forces in those awful days of the Winnipeg strike is of more than local" political significance. A great principle is involved; a principle that no minister of the crown, not even a government, should be allowed to profane.
Last year a considerable item was included on the estimates to adjust the salaries of and compensate a number of the strikers dismissed from the service during the Winnipeg strike. Opposition to the measure was so strong in the commons that the item was finally struck out of the estimates and the Postmaster General executed a temporary retreat. This year, however, a bill is under consideration, and parliament will be asked to vote approximately $125,000 to reinstate and reimburse the strikers.
Anyone acquainted with the efforts put forth to prevent utter demoralization of public services in the city of Winnipeg during the hectic days of the strike is aware of the masterly manner in which Thomas Bower, postmaster at the time, kept the mail moving and prevented a total tie-up of the service that affected not only the city, but the prairie provinces as well. Mr Bower consistently refused to reinstate the striking post office employees and give them seniority over the staunch supporters who

Western Postal
Employees-Mt. Bennett
remained loyal to the crown and, even in the face of serious danger to themselves, remained long hours at their posts and made it possible for the office to function. Now as a reward for this service to the state, the Honourable Peter Veniot has forced a vacation and ultimate retirement oil the postmaster at \ymnipeg, for the purpose, obviously, of making it easier to reinstate the strikers and thus consummate some political bargain with the Labour party.
The postmaster at Winnipeg has been released from dutv in a manner quite characteristic of Honourable Mr. ATeniot's administration of the department. But the reinstatement of strikers and adjustment of salaries fortunately require a vote of money in the commons, and this provides the opportunity for the people of Canada, through their representatives in parliament, to rebuke the Postmaster General and put a stop to his high-handed political manoeuvering This abject surrender to the Winnipeg Labour party *would be an unpardonable affront to everyone who remained loyal to state laws and state institutions and struggled against fearful odds in 1919 to maintain them. More than that, anv officer of the crown merits and must have, in the honest and conscientious pursuit of his duties, the unfaltering support of the department of government under which he labours. That is one of the tenets of successful business and sound government administration. These principles the Postmaster General would violate for a mess of political pottage.
Without partisanship or political affiliations "The Farmers's Advocate" is forced to condemn untoward action in any administration. Principle is above party. The people, in the last analysis, are supreme.	,,	,
Under our system of government the people, fortunately, have a means of expression; and the opportunity here presents itself, before it is too late, to demand adherence to principle and honour in the conduct of public affairs.
As I have said, that article appears in an independent newspaper which in times past could not be charged with any particular lack of appreciation of the sendees rendered to the state by the government.
In common, I suppose, with most of the other members of the house, I have received a photographic copy of issues of the Western Labour News, taken from the provincial library of Manitoba. This was sent with the compliments of the Employers' Association of Manitoba, the prairie division of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Winnipeg board of trade, the Winnipeg builders' exchange and the Winnipeg realty exchange. These articles are four in number, the first one being dated May 17, 1919. The opening sentence is:
How does the idea of using the new- parliament buildings for a labour temple strike you?

speechtext:
The sentences may have
been quoted apart from their contexts, but it seems to me I hat the sentence "How does the idea of using the new parliament buildings for a labour temple strike you? is certainly a sentence complete within itself. Another paragraph quoted is:
It is reported that certain rigs are delivering ice. bread, etc., without the printed card authorized by the strike committee, borne ot these carry written notices. We warn all such drivers that this is contrary to the orders ot the strike committee. Certified permits will be supplied on request by the food committee.
Another paragraph is:
Theatres and picture shows are running under strike permit so that the workers can keep off the streets.
Another one is:
All these concerns are organized fully and could be stopped on a minute's notice, but tor the present the strike committee believes that it is better to let them run-hence its order for them to stay on the job under permit.
Edition No. 2 contains this paragraph:
All telegraphers are out on strike. But. in order to avert unnecessary hardship, such men as are absolutely necessary have been sent back under strike permit to send out such wires as are passed by strike committee.
Special strike edition No. 8 contains the following:
The postal federation and the telephone operators have received their ultimatums. We wonder why they delayed so long to do this. Tn a few hours more it may be expected that the city council will do the same thing re its employees. Then the individual employers will
follow suit.	.	i _
The reply of labour is explicit. No worker will return to work until the principle ot collective bargaining and a living wage is recognized.
Then follows a paragraph from the last issue, as follows:
What will the governments, and the city councils, and the railroads, and the private
Western Postal

Employees-Mr. Bennett
bosses do? Not a single worker will go back till all are reinstated. The governments say that their employees are dismissed and that their dismissals are final. Then the issue is clear. Either the governments must eat humble pie or they must resign.
They have no other choice. Labour comprises the majority of the population. The 1,000 are so insignificant that it would need a magnifying glass to see them. It looks as if they will have to abandon the field and let their governments resign.
I think the sentences which I have just read are complete within themselves. I read them because they indicate the conditions which prevailed before and after the postal workers left their employment. The hon. minister quoted from an order in council which was passed in June, 1920, which contains very significant words; The ordler in council sets out the fact that it was a "sympathetic strike" under which the postal workers left their employment, that they were advised of "the gravity of their offence against 'the state," but that "clemency" would be extended consistent with "maintaining the necessary discipline." According to the admissions of the minister, it was a sympathetic strike which induced the postal men to quit their employment and tie up the postal service of Winnipeg. It is apparent that they left for no grievance of their own-they had none at the time-'but rather because others had grievances and they were in sympathy with them. I think that is abundantly clear from what the minister has said.
Then it occurs to me that we have to ask a very simple question. Is the attitude of the government different from that taken by most employers under similar circumstances?
I received, I dare say in company with other members of the house, a resolution passed by a body of locomotive engineers. It was signed by at least one engineer whom I know and I recall that within a very short space of time prior to that he with others had called upon me asking me if I could not use my influence, such as it was, for the purpose of helping them in seeking employment, not as engineers, but as men who had ceased to be in the service, because they had been dismissed for what their fellow employees said were just causes, as hostlers or in some other branch of the service of a great railway corporation, regardless of the fact that they were as well able to render service as engineers as they ever were. Having committed an offence against the rules of the corporation they had been dismissed :rom the service and now they sought reemployment not as engineers, with all the knowledge they had of that business, but in any capacity in which they could find employment as beginners in the service. They said 
very frankly that some of those who had been dismissed should not be entrusted again with a locomotive hauling a passenger train.
Need I remind the house that during the Great war, aye, prior to the Great war, we have the history of a great soldier who for an offence was cashiered from the British army. He volunteered as a private in a foreign army, rose to a position of great importance and became a commander. During the war I recall perhaps not many but some similar instances at least. I remember in particular one who was a friend of mine, who has since passed to his reward. He was employed as an officer. For good and sufficient causes he was dismissed from his position, and he enrolled as a private. He began again to work his way up the ladder to place and position in the force of which he was a member. So it is all through life. I venture to point it out in these words, words which I think we all have to keep in mind because we all at one time or another realize the soundness of them:
hot heaven itself upon the past has power, out what has been, has been.
The fact is that these unfortunate men, for sympathetic reasons only, left the employ of the state, tied up and dislocated the postal service of Winnipeg and, when they were afforded an opportunity to go back and be reinstated, declined to do so. When the period was extended; when the government saw fit to say to them: You may have a longer time in which to make up your mind, a number of them still declined to make up their minds to go back into the service of the state. Under those circumstances the question is: Have they a claim for retroactive pay from this parliament? Under the conditions mentioned iby the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), have they a right now, seeing that they joined as new employees, to ask parliament to make them employees as from the date of their first employment, without taking into consideration any breach of employment or any time during which they were not employed? The principle is very far-reaching. Think what it means to this country to have the House of Commons declare to-day that men who were employed many years ago, who left their employment for sympathetic reasons, who declined to go back having two opportunities to do so, and who then went back under a distinct contract with the state that when they did so they joined as new employees, are now to be told that they are to be treated as though they had never left the service,^ as though there had never been a break in their employment, as though they had never gone on a sympathetic strike. I

for one cannot bring myself to that state of mind. When I remember the statements that have been made to me by dismissed employees of corporations in this country who have sought my assistance that they might get back to any employment, and who have gladly gone back to subordinate positions, positions where men who were once their juniors became their seniors and their superintendents,
I also remember that we do not take, with relation to ordinary transactions, the action that is now proposed. I remember further that, according to the very language of the Free Press newspaper, we put the imprimatur of the approval of this parliament upon the validity of that strike. As the House of Commons of Canada we will have said that that sympathetic strike was justified; that the leaving of their employment by the postal workers was justified, and that the consequences which follow every man for his act shall not follow in this particular case. As I have said, I cannot bring myself to agree to that reasoning. As a citizen, as a lawyer, as a member of parliament, I cannot give my assent to such propositions.
But let us for a moment ask us these further questions before we leave that phase of the matter. First, ninety-six men were employed by the state in the postal service.
Did they leave the service? Answer, yes.
Have they a grievance against the state that employed them? Answer, no.
Did they leave for sympathetic reasons because of grievances that others alleged they had? Answer, yes.
Were they afforded an opportunity for reinstatement? Answer, yes.
Did they avail themselves of it? Answer, no.
Were they afforded a further opportunity for reinstatement? Answer, yes.
Did they avail themselves of it? Answer, no.
Did they subsequently request the government to reemploy them? Answer, yes.
Was that request granted? Answer, yes.
By what method? Answer, by an order in council just read by the minister.
Did it impose conditions? Answer, it did.
W7as one of those conditions that they should be treated as new employees? Answer, yes.
Under those circumstances we are asked to disregard period of the unemployment and reinstate them in salary. They have already had many of the other benefits, and reinstatement as regards salary means putting them in the position as though they had never left

speechtext:
I mean from the date
of reemployment. I mean from the day they went to work after the strike, the day of reemployment after the strike. While, as I have said, I find it difficult to think that any government would' submit such a measure to parliament, it has been done, and we have to meet the situation. We who sit to the left of the Speaker are not unmindful of the fact that at the time of these unfortunate occurrences, the Hon, Gideon Robertson, who has been a supporter of those who sit to the left of the Speaker, was Minister of Labour. He visited Winnipeg at that time, under circumstances to which I referred last year and with which I shall not trouble the house again. I thought it desirable, in view of my inability to arrive at any conclusion that would permit me to support this measure in justice to my fellow-citizens, in justice to my fellow-Canadians in every walk of life, to consult with him, and he made to me a suggestion which I shall give to this house for what it is worth. Senator Robertson, being very familiar with the matter, suggested that after all punishment should not be eternal- none of us believes in eternal punishment. One of my colleagues suggests that there are still some who do believe in eternal punishment, but certainly my friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and I do not. It is now ten years since these men left the service and Senator Robertson suggested that as a period of ten years had since elapsed, justice would be done if those who had attained to the position which it was contended from their long service they were entitled, on recommendations made by their superior officers on the basis of their merit, regardless of the years of employment, received the increased salary up to the maximum of their class. I have thought over this suggestion very carefully.

speechtext:
That is the ground which was urged by the Postmaster General and by the hon. gentleman last year, and which is urged again here to-day. Of course you cannot apply that principle in life. The demoted officer was a better private than any other private in the battalion because of his knowledge; the demoted officer who went into the Egyptian army was a better man than the other men in that army, and rose to be its commander; the demoted locomotive engineer became a better hostler than the men engaged in that work; the demoted conductor who became a brakeman was a better brakeman because of his past experience. But in the particular cases to which I referred, these employees of a private corporation lost their seniority, their pensions, and their claims to consideration on the part of 
their employers, and now I say that in order to end this matter, in order to have it no longer dragged into parliament as it has been under the circumstances alluded to by the Postmaster General, in order to prevent these acrimonious discussions to which the Free Press refers, in order that it may not be said that one party in the strike triumphed over the other-which is, after all, apparently what is to be done-in order to prevent all that, I thought the suggestion of Senator Robertson not an unreasonable one. If therefore the government were disposed to provide that from a future date, on the recommendation of their superior officers as to the character of the service rendered, those employees who had terminated their employment and afterwards been reemployed by a contract of re-employment which is fixed by order in council should receive this increased compensation, we on this side would not be unwilling that they should receive that consideration which their superior officers might recommend, in the light of the services they had rendered counted in years of service without regard to any interruption that had taken place in it. That is the best compromise suggestion, if you call it such-because after all, statecraft they say is always compromise-that we can make. Neither as a lawyer nor as a citizen nor as a member of this parliament could I legally become a party to it, but because of a very earnest desire to bring about happy and peaceful relations between the state as employer and the postal workers as employees and to prevent the harrowing discussions that take place in this parliament with respect to what happened ten years ago, the then Minister of Labour, who has as warm a heart for the men who toil as any man in this Dominion, has offered this suggestion, and after listening to his observations and his reasons I am convinced that it would be fair solution of what is a difficult problem. It is a compromise, it is true, but it violates no principle. It places no imprimatur of the approval of this parliament upon the validity or invalidity of what has been done in days gone by. It leaves out all the harrowing discussions with respect to the strike. It does not deal with the problems of re-instatement or re-employment, but leaves the question to be considered whether or not in the light of the greater experience of the worker he is entitled to receive greater compensation than the one who has less experience in that particular class of work, although it is perfectly clear that in the ten years that have elapsed the new men who have come in must

speechtext: May I ask my hoD. friend one question? It is a little aside from what he is discussing. As a matter of fact, my understanding would be that as the War Measures Act was still in force, the wide provisions of that act enabled the order in council to be passed. I only say that to the right hon. gentleman because I asked the same question in relation to it, and that is the only answer I have at the moment. The War Measures Act conferred on the executive almost legislative-some have said wholly legislative-powers, in many regards. They thus had power, without coming to parliament, to override the provisions of the Civil Service Act to that extent. The men still had to pass examinations; the age limit was disregarded. Then they had to have the approval of the governor in council with respect to every specific case of employment. Lastly, they came in as new employees.
Now, I submit, the question is a very simple one. Why should parliament overlook the fact that the men themselves terminated their employment? Nobody asked
2258	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
them to leave the service. They did a grievous injury to the body politic by leaving their employment. What is more, it was stated in that order in council, and I once more direct attention to these words, that, first of all, it was a "sympathetic strike" that prevailed in Winnipeg; secondly, "they now realize the gravity of their offence against the state." Now we are going to reward them for realizing "the gravity of their offence against the state" by saying that they are to get full pay from the moment they went back to employment, regardless of the fact that they themselves acknowledge they were guilty of a grave offence against the state? That is what it gets down to.
It is my earnest desire, as I have said, to promote amity and good feeling between the great body of civil servants of this country and the state that employs them. Having had the benefit of a discussion with the gentleman whom I regard as being more fitted [DOT] to speak in relation to the matter than anyone else that we have in parliament at the moment, I can only say that the compromise as such violates no principle. It merely says that if the postmaster, or whoever is the superior officer, reports with respect to fitness, he shall not be limited by reason of the fact that these men have been in the employment of the department during a limited number of years, that having been in the post office before 1919 they have more experience by reason of that fact, and that experience shall be taken into account to increase their compensation or salary-not retroactively, not as a reward for their grave offence against the state, but at a future date, to be fixed either by the governor in council or by this parliament, in satisfaction of these long outstanding claims, in the hope that this action may change to some degree of harmony what has been a very discordant note in the history of this young country.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset congratulate the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on the comparatively moderate tone of his contribution to the debate as compared with the tone of his remarks on this subject last session. I am very strongly in favour of this resolution as it stands. I think that the criticism which has been directed against it has been based upon a misconception of its purposes and a misunderstanding of the situation in Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Calgary and Vancouver which it is designed to correct. When that situation is 
clearly understood and the purposes of this resolution are fully appreciated, I think the resolution will commend itself to the members of this house.
In order to make the situation a little more clear and to meet some of the objections that have been raised against this proposal, I think certain facts ought to be brought to the attention of the house. It will not be possible in the short space of time at my disposal to deal with all the aspects of the question which have been brought up, but I intend to ideal iwith the more important ones at this stage and then when the house is in committee I shall be able to deal more fully with other aspects.
The postal employees of western Canada in 1919 belonged to an organization called the Amalgamated Postal Workers. The Winnipeg branch of that organization was and had been for some time affiliated with the Trades and Labour Council of Winnipeg. The fact of that affiliation was well known to the post office authorities at that time. When the general strike was called on May 15th, 1919, the Winnipeg branch of the Amalgamated Postal Workers went out, as did many other labour unions affiliated with the Trades and Labour Council of Winnipeg, and the strike spread to the post offices of Saskatoon and Calgary.
On May 24, when the strike had been in progress for some nine days, an ultimatum was issued by the postmaster at Winnipeg, on behalf of the government, to the postal workers who had gone on strike. The essential part of that ultimatum reads as follows:
To-day voluntary workers are temporarily taking the posts these people have left. The government announces that those returning before 12 o'clock noon on Monday the 26th instant, will he accepted and that all failing to resume their duties by that hour will be definitely refused thereafter a place in the federal service. Commencing at the above stated hour new employees will be engaged on the usual permanent basis.
It. will be noticed that this ultimatum was delivered on the 24th of May, a public holiday. It was also a Saturday and it called upon the employees to return to duty by noon of the following Monday. A number did return to duty but a great many did not. Those who did not return were removed from the postal service by two orders in council, the first being P.C. 89-1474, dated July 15, and the second, P.C. 2224, dated November 3. This latter dealt with those who had not been covered by the former. The ultimatum which I read a moment ago definitely notified the postal workers that if they did not return

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Thorson
before a certain hour they would be definitely refused thereafter a place in the federal service; that is, the federal service was to be closed to them completely.
I am trying to give the facts to the house fully so that the record may be accurate and as complete as I can make it. Representations were made on behalf of these men to the authorities at Ottawa with regard to the terms of the ultimatum. Many of these men had been trusted employees; they had been efficient and conscientious servants of the public; many of them were returned soldiers who had recently been demobilized and had returned to the postal service shortly before the general strike. The government listened to these representations and appointed a subcommittee of council consisting of the Hon. P. E. Blondin, who was then Postmaster General, and the Hon. G. D. Robertson, who was then Minister of Labour, to look into the whole question and see whether some solution of the difficulty could not be found. These two ministers prepared a memorandum to the Civil Service Commission dated January 7, 1920, and presented it to the Hon. N. W. Rowell, who was then president of the privy council. That memorandum was accepted by council and became the basis for the reemployment of the men who had been dismissed. Perhaps I might read it and comment upon some of its' terms. It is dated January 7, 1920, is entitled "Memorandum to the Civil Service Commissioners," and reads as follows:
Many evidences have reached the Department of Labour from ex-postal employees that they now recognize they participated unwisely in the sympathetic strike in western Canada last May, and that they sincerely regret the action they then took. The gravity of their offence against the state being now realized, the government has given consideration to the possibility of removing the bar to their application through the Civil Service Commission for reemployment in the public service, and His Excellency the Governor in Council is disposed to exercise clemency so far as reasonably consistent with necessary discipline.
Ex-postal employees may therefore be considered as eligible to be appointed to positions in the civil service for which they make application as vacancies occur, and to which, in the opinion of the commission, they are justly entitled under the regulations, subject to the following conditions:
Then three conditions are enumerated:
Ex-postal workers must not be reemployed in the civil service without the approval in each case of His Excellency the Governor in Council;
Inasmuch as a number of those affected have been a long time in the public service, and are now past the age limit fixed for new employees entering the service, it will be permissible for the commission to appoint them notwithstanding the age requirements.
In every case before being reappointed satisfactory assurance must be obtained that a repetition of the offence will not occur.
The only two conditions of reemployment referred to in this memorandum are that in each case approval by order in council must be obtained and satisfactory assurance must be given that a repetition of the offence will not occur. In other words, the government was prepared to recede from the position it had taken in the ultimatum, that these men would be forever barred from tlhe federal service; it came to a different decision, namely, that they might be reemployed in the federal service subject to certain conditions. I think the government took a very fair-minded attitude to the general situation and I should like to commend it for so doing. However, in my opinion, as I shall point out later, it did not go far enough.
In consequence of this change in the attitude of the government a number of men have been reemployed in the federal sendee notwithstanding the terms of the ultimatum of May 24, 1919, and I wish to emphasize this-that all the men who have been so reemployed have been specially approved by order in council; all of them have given satisfactory assurance that the offence for which they were dismissed will not be repeated.
In respect of all the ninety-six men who were dismissed and are now back in the service there are orders in council; so far as I can ascertain the first of these orders is P.C. 1152, dated June 4, 1920, which reads as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 31st May, 1920, from the Secretary of State, submitting that the Civil Service Commission has recently received applications for positions in the civil service from ex-postal employees who participated in the sympathetic strike in western Canada in the spring of 1919. In accordance with the understanding arrived at by the government, as embodied in a memorandum forwarded to the Civil Service Commission by Senator Robertson on the 7th January, 1920, ex-postal employees are to be considered eligible for appointment to positions in the civil service, subject to certain conditions therein mentioned. The ex-postal employees mentioned in the attached list have complied with the conditions of this memorandum. The minister, therefore, recommends that authority be granted for the appointment of these candidates to positions for which they are eligible. The committee advise that the requisite authority be granted accordingly.

2260	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Thorson
noticed, Mr. Speaker, that order in council P.C. 1152, to which I referred a moment ago, incorporated the memorandum to the Civil Service Commission of January 7, 1920, in which reference was made to only two conditions, first that re-employment should be subject to approval by order in council and secondly that the men should give satisfactory assurance that they would not again participate in a sympathetic strike. The other consequences of their re-employment followed by reason of defects in the Civil Service Act with regard to re-employment, which this bill is designed to correct.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: May I ask a question?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I have only forty minutes; I would like to finish this part of my argument and then I shall be glad to answer questions.
In all there are now 79 men in the Winnipeg post office who were dismissed by reason of their participation in the general strike. There are also a few such men at Saskatoon, Calgary and Vancouver. I should like the house to take note of the numbers in which these men came back into the service. Of the 79 men in Winnipeg 35 came back in 1920, a year after the strike; 11 came back in 1921, 10 in 1922, 14 in 1923, 6 in 1925 and one in each of the years 1926, 1927 and 1928.
I should like to point out also that the regulations regarding the re-employment of these men, which were framed in 1920, are still in force. The government in 1920 reserved to itself the right to determine whether or not a man should be re-employed in the federal service. That right is still reserved; this resolution does not affect it at all. The memorandum of January 7, 1920, proposed that appointments should be made only as vacancies occurred, and that these appointments should be made by the Civil Service Commission. This resolution is not intended to change that procedure in any way. There is not a single man in the employ of the Dominion government either in the Winnipeg post office or elsewhere who will be prejudiced in the slightest degree by effect being given to the resolution now before the house.
I have endeavoured to outline very briefly the steps which led to the dismissal of these postal employees and to the framing of the regulations for their re-employment. I commend the action of the government of that day, a Conservative government, in going as far as it did; I think it acted in a humanitarian way, but I have one criticism to offer.
I think every member of this house will agree that the government of Canada should

#
set an example for other employers of labour to follow, and I was very glad indeed to have for that proposition the approval of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) who stated the other evening that the Dominion government should be a model employer. The Dominion government should at least be as fair to its employees as other employers of labour were to theirs. What happened? These men who were taken back into the employ of the government were in most cases, particularly in 1920 and 1921, put back at the identical work they had been doing previously; full use was made by the Dominion government of their training, their experience and their efficiency. This is not a case of rewarding these men for something they did not do but rather a case of paying them what they have already earned but have not received.
I have here a statement showing in detail with respect to the 79 men who were dismissed from the service by reason of their participation in the strike of 1919 and are now back on the staff of the Winnipeg post office, their length of service, their classification or rank and the salary they were receiving prior to their dismissal. Of these 79 men 20 had been in the service of the Post Office Department ten years or more at the time of their dismissal, and their average length of service was over eight years. I think that is proof that it was the trained, experienced, capable men who wanted to get back into the postal service and who were accepted into that service. This was the result of the policy of requiring approval by order in council in each case where these men were re-employed. Their classifications ranged from the lowest to the highest, from that of transfer agent to that of a comparatively high class clerk, and their salaries ranged all the way from $1,180 per year including bonus to $1,830 per year, including bonus.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That was before the strike?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Yes. Yet what happened? These men were all taken back as new employees. Notwithstanding their length of service, their training, their experience, the fact that they were put to the same work after the strike as they had' been doing before it, notwithstanding their classifications and the salaries they had been receiving, they were all taken back as new employees at the lowest grade in the postal service and at the minimum salary of the lowest grade. They did the same work, particularly those taken back in 1920 and 1921, after they were taken back into the service as they had been doing prior to their dismissal. Let me take as an example

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Thorson
the man whose name appears first on this list which I have before me. At the time of his dismissal he had served thirteen years in the Post Office Department; he occupied the rank of a high class clerk and received a salary of $1,830, including the bonus which was paid at that time. That man went on strike in May of 1919 and was taken back into the service on September 7, 1920. When he was taken back into the service he was placed at exactly the same work he had been doing previous to his dismissal; the value of his services to the state was just as great in 1920 as it had been in 1919! Why should he be paid differently? What happened to this man? He had been receiving $1,830 per year, which was the estimate which the state itself put upon his services, but when he came back he was taken on as a postal helper and paid $85 per month.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: And doing the same work.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
And doing the same work which he had been doing. I appeal to the sense of justice and fair play which exists in the mind of every member of this house and ask them to say whether that was fair. Are we going to rest upon an imperfection in the law when that imperfection can be cured? I say that the government of the day should have gone further and done what other employers did, even if it meant an amendment of the existing law.
What does the resolution which is now before the house propose to do? Simply this: that the postal employees shall be paid by the Dominion of Canada for the services which they have rendered according to the value of such services. The principle of the resolution is this: that the Dominion government should do as other employers of labour did and recognize the fundamental principle, of which the Postmaster General spoke, that the labourer is worthy of his hire. The government should pay its postal employees in Winnipeg and elsewhere what they have actually already earned. That is all that was involved in the item in the supplementary estimates last year. That is the fundamental principle underlying this resolution and every member of the house can accept that prin-liple as being sound and just.
Since the time at my disposal does not permit me to deal with it in detail, I shall deal very briefly with the argument of the hon. deader of the opposition. Why should not the Dominion government treat its former employees who went on strike as other employers
of labour treated theirs? It was quite within the rights of the railway companies not to reemploy their striking conductors; likewise it was quite within the rights of the Dominion government not to reemploy its postal employees who had gone on strike. They both did so, however, and in so doing they acted in a humanitarian way. We commend the railway companies for acting as they did, and we commend the Dominion government for its action, but there is this great difference between the action of the Dominion government and the action of the private railway companies; when the railway companies took back their conductors and used them as conductors they paid them the wages of a conductor and not the wages of a wiper; they paid them the wages of a conductor because that was what they were worth to them. What did the Dominion government do? It took back its postal employees, used their training and experience, had the full benefit of their services to the state, and paid them as green hands. What did employers of labour generally do? The employers of carpenters, masons, mechanics and other skilled workmen reemployed their men who had gone on strike as they saw fit; it is quite true that not all of them were reemployed, but tbpse who were reemployed were taken back at the current rate of wages-they were not paid as apprentices. Yet the Dominion government in all cases, regardless of the value of the services which these men were performing, paid them as green hands, as beginners in the service.
This resolution proposes to do two things; first of all, to pay these men as from the date of their re-employment the salary they would have received had they been taken back into the service at the salary they were receiving prior to their dismissal.

speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to ask it after my time has expired? The resolution proposes also to put the government in the position which it would have occupied had it followed the example of other employers of labour.
I should like to deal with one more point, since it has been raised. It has been said that the approval of this resolution involves a justification of the strike. When, a year ago, I was discussing the item in the supplementary estimates relating to this question, I said that I did not intend to discuss the merits or demerits of the general strike of

2262	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Thorson
1919 in which these men had participated. I do mot intend to do so to-day; I do not think that the merits or demerits of the strike are in any way involved in the great principle that the labourer is worthy of his hire, and that the Dominion government should pay for services rendered according to the value of such services. Whether the strike was right or wrong, if a man was worth a certain sum of money in 1919 before the strike, then in 1920, after the strike, when he was domg the same kind of work as he had been doing before, he was worth just as much then as he was worth before. That is all that is involved. He is the same man, the value of his services to the state are the same; the value of his services to the state did not decrease merely because he participated in a general strike, perhaps after being unwisely advised. I take the view, notwithstanding the editorial in the Free Press-for the. editor of which I have a very high regard-that the questions involved in the general strike are in no way involved in this resolution. There is only one principle involved in this resolution. I have enunciated that principle several times.
May I refer, Mr. Speaker, to a precedent for the application of this general principle? I see no reason why this principle should be applied in the case of the Toronto strikers, who took part in the strike of 1924, and not applied in the case of the Winnipeg strikers, who took part in the strike of 1919. I know it will be said that in the case of the Toronto strikers the men were striking in respect of i grievance of their own and that in the case >f the Winnipeg strike it was a sympathetic strike and the men had no grievance of their own. I do not agree that that is altogether so, out I have not time to deal with that argument at this stage of the discussion. After all, the principle is the same; the men went on strike contrary to the terms of an ultimatum similar to that delivered at Winnipeg, and they were dismissed from the service, as the Winnipeg men had been dismissed; they were re-employed as postal helpers, as the Winipeg men had been re-employed. Yet, on March 20, 1926, the Hon. Charles Murphy, who was then postmaster general, listened to the representations which were made on behalf of the Toronto strikers and applied to them the same principle which we are asking this house to apply to the Winnipeg strikers. That principle was this: that these men were doing the same kind of work as before the strike and they should be paid accordingly. Hon. Mr. Murphy ordered that the Toronto strikers who had been taken back should be paid as from the date of their re-employment the

salary which they had been receiving at the time of their dismissal from the service. In this connection I should like to commend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). I think he has taken a very sympathetic attitude towards this question, and the principle that is involved. During the course of the election campaign of 1926 he paid us in Winnipeg a memorable visit which was much appreciated by many members on this side of the house. In the course of his visit to Winnipeg he had occasion, I believe, to meet a committee of the postal workers in the Winnipeg post office who had been dismissed because of their participation in the strike and who were back in the service. He was then Postmaster General, and I assume that in the attitude which he took towards that committee he was acting for the government of which he was then a member. The committee laid before him the facts of the Toronto strike: they explained to him the action which had been taken by the Hon. Charles Murphy, in 1926. I am told that the hon. member for Fort William in his capacity as Postmaster General told these men that, in his opinion, from the facts laid before him, their application Should be and would be favourably considered if the government of which he was a member should be sustained at the forthcoming election.

Then I think I may agree with the hon. member in these remarks. After all, the principle is the same even though the causes of the strikes were different. The Dominion government is proposing to pay these men for services rendered; it does not intend to give them something for nothing. The position that we have taken all along in connection with this resolution is that these men have earned what we now propose to pay them.
This resolution may now affect directly only very few men, but it will be of interest to many because of the nature of the principle involved. We on this side of the house do not intend to limit our efforts to do full justice and to follow the example of other employers of labour by reason of imperfections in the law if we can correct those imperfections by an act such as we now propose to have passed with the consent of the house.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house another feature of the matter. Canada has taken a very prominent place in the International Labour Organization which has its office at Geneva. Anyone who has heard our Canadian representatives speak of Canada's attitude at Geneva in international labour matters must be proud of the part that she has played. If we are to continue our pride in Canada's achievements, in Canada's attitude in labour matters, how can we justify that pride if Canada is not willing to follow the example of other employers of labour in recognizing the fundamental principle that the labourer is worthy of his hire whether he went on strike or not; that services should be paid for according to their value?
When the Hon. Charles Murphy adjusted the salaries of the postal workers in Toronto in 1926, he bad in mind the creation of greater harmony, greater cooperation between the government and its employees and increased efficiency in the public service. If this resolution is put into effect, I think it will pay handsome dividends to the public in the way of increased harmony, increased cooperation and greater efficiency of service. We should 78594-1431
all like to hear the last of the Winnipeg strike in this house, but we shall not do so as long as there are grievances to be remedied and the men involved in that strike who are back in the service still have a grievance. The passing of this resolution will remove that grievance and we from Winnipeg ask the members of this house to assist us in writing the last chapter of that great strike. I hope, when that last chapter is written, it will be entitled "Justice to the postal employees of the Dominion government."

The hon. gentleman mentioned that I met the strikers in Winnipeg during the last election campaign, and he is quite correct in that. I met them as one member of the cabinet and as Postmaster General of that day. I have always felt very friendly toward labour, I have always desired and I desire now to take what is a fair-minded Christian attitude towards a group of men like this; I say that sincerely. My attitude towards them when I met them in Winnipeg was this, that I was only one member of the cabinet, that I could nOt definitely promise anything, because being only one I was subject to the opinion of the whole cabinet, but I promised that if we were returned to power I would give most fair consideration to their demands after looking thoroughly into the case. Naturally I had to hear the other side of the case before I could commit even myself to anything, let alone the rest of the government. I certainly intended if we were returned to power to give their case fair consideration, and certainly so far as I am concerned I am willing to go as far as most men in a case of this kind. solution. I take the position that no government can afford to deal lightly or negligently with the tremendous principle involved, namely, the question of the public service. I realized when in Manitoba how throughout the country we were all affected by this strike. The whole of the postal service was disorganized, and, in the country of which I can speak, they were entirely hostile to all the principles involved in that strike. Having experienced the effects of the strike, and coming now to the question of settlement, there is not a man either in this house or elsewhere who would not wish that these postal strikers should be sympathetically dealt with. But unfortunately individuals must suffer in the general application of law; for no law ever was evolved whereby everyone benefits: in the application of the law some hardship is suffered by individuals. Now these individuals took upon themselves to enter a strike and they have been penalized. I am not going to deal at any length with all that has been said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) or by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson), but I take this postion:	In view of the fact that
these men had twice an opportunity to go back, which opportunity was not accepted; that they then had a meeting with the Hon. Gideon Robertson; that a memorandum was submitted to the government of the day admitting that they had seen the gravity of their offence, and that when the reinstatement took place they entered into a contract wheTe-in they undertook to perform the services which they had formerly rendered' on the condition laid down in the Civil Service Act, namely, that they were really new entrants into the postal service-a contract which they knew at the time carried only that minimum wage of the lower grade-and that they were satisfied to go back into the service on these terms, I must take the ground that, having done so, they must now suffer the consequences. Like the leader of the opposition however, and for the sake of compromise in the settlement of what is a very vexed question throughout the west and in Manitoba particularly, I think the bill might be amended so 'that these men who are receiving benefits to-day should also receive that seniority which would entitle them to further benefits. That would be a gracious act. I know it is in the very spirit of compromise. Of course, we cannot always be strictly logical in these matters, and I am glad to see the leader of the opposition taking that point of view, although the other night he was not so keen for it. I do think, however, that in this case a compromise might be accepted by the postal
workers in Winnipeg, recognizing them in the position they now occupy. The heat and passionate feeling in relation to that strike have to a large extent evaporated. No one wishes to revive those feelings. On the other hand, certainly no one wishes to create a precedent which will enable persons in the service in the future to come to parliament and say, "You did this for the strikers of 1919; you reinstated them, recompensing them for the loss of wages. And now we wish also to have that precedent considered as a basis for a similar claim in our behalf". If a precedent were created, strikers in the future would feel entitled to come to parliament and seek to have that precedent invoked to their advantage. I think it might be well for the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) to take into consideration the proposal that has been put forward. Certainly if the matter goes through in the form intended I shall vote against it.

Like otheTs who have spoken with reference to this bill, I am sympathetic so far as certain parts of it are concerned. I too think that the time is coming, in fact it is here, when, in the words of Lord Robert Cecil, we must get away from the war mind. No doubt until this time a great many members of this house would have opposed this bill in its entirety, and the fact that the leader of the opposition and many others on this side of the house have gone as far as they have is, I think, evidence on the part of the people of this country that, more or less, bygones should be bygones and that as far as possible peace and harmony should be restored.
At the same time I must agree with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) and the leader of the opposition. The leader of the opposition has gone a great way in compromising to the extent he has; because, try as we may, we cannot dissociate this question from the cause of the Winnipeg strike. It is all very well for any hon. member to say he will not discuss the merits of the strike, that he does not wish to discuss it, that he does not wish either to justify or to condemn it. So say we all; we do not even like to raise the question. But when you are wiping out the penalty entirely as we are here doing, and putting these men back in the status they would have had if they had never gone on strike, we are by that very act justifying their course in striking; we are saying that what they did in 1919 was right and that the conditions laid down by parliament and in the order in council which has been read here were wrong. We are saying that parliament

There was a man who served in the South African war and who later became an employee in the Calgary post office; he was a letter sorter, I believe, and supported his wife and small family. He went out on the sympathetic strike and then had to leave the country, because there were no vacancies and he could not get a job. He went to California, but before leaving he saw me and explained the situation. He had purchased some property; they placed a mortgage on that property and as far as I know they have not returned to Canada, unless they have done so within the last few months. That man lost his job because he went out on the sympathetic strike, and there were no vacancies which he could fill. The result is that so far as the public service is concerned he is done for; he is getting old and his eyesight is failing.
On the other hand the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre referred' to a man in Winnipeg who was re-emplbyed by the Post Office department more than a year after the strike, I believe sometime in the fall of 1920. A vacancy occurred; he pased the examination, was selected for the position and entered the service at a certain rate of pay. There is a fact which it seems to me must not be overlooked; that man need not have re-entered the service at that rate of pay had he not desired to do so. Being twenty-one years of age and a man of experience, without the least coercion being applied he agreed

speechtext: Then when he went back in 1920, what did he get? I understand that there were 79 cases in Winnipeg, one or two cases in Calgary and some in Saskatoon, making a total of 90. Now I want to know when these men being over twenty-one years of age went to work under a definite contract with the state, a contract which they made freely and voluntarily, without threat, without duress, without misrepresentation and without coercion; a contract under which they agreed to work for so many dollars a month. I want to know the dates when they went back to work, how many increases they have received since that time, and how many of these men are now receiving the maximum salaries of their classes. That is, how many of these men have had their services recognized according to the provisions of the Civil Service Act so that they have reached the maximum of their class? That is important, because if they have been promoted that shows a recognition of their meritorious services, and there is nothing to indicate that those promotions were not based upon their efficiency in the light of their experience. In other words, we do not want to do this thing twice. These promotions have been obtained on the certificate of their superior officer, who certifies upon his honour, without regard to political or other considerations that such and such a man has rendered meritorious service and is entitled to his increase. I want to know how many of these men have reached their maximums and are receiving what they would have received had they never terminated their employment with the state. Then there is a further answer which suggests itself, and which is very simple: Why did he not think of that when he refused to go back to work? Even assuming that to be so, he must suffer the consequences of so standing out, and one consequence was that he went back to work under this new contract.
There is just one observation which I cannot permit to pass unchallenged. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre keeps dwelling upon the fact that a man should receive compensation in proportion to the service rendered, but let me put another proposition to this house. Take the case of a new man standing by, doing his job without complaint; he had broken no contract and had dislocated no service. Perhaps he was a returned soldier, since many of the employees taken on at that time were returned men. Then another man reenters the service; he had broken his contract with the state; he had dislocated the service, and now he stands side by side with that other man, as a beginner under a contract into which he entered freely and voluntarily. So we have two beginners, A and B; one had broken no contract, had participated in no sympathetic strike and had done nothing to disturb the service of the country. They worked together, and it is said that one could and did do more work than the other, but they were both paid at the same rate. I know of no place in the world, in any kind of employment, where that condition is not found. There is always one man who does a little more, and he is the man who usually emerges as superintendent, as foreman or perhaps as president of the organization. But now we are told that we are to make a new contract for

one man but not for the other, regardless of the services which have been rendered by this other new man, who is ambitious, who has been toiling hard and who wants to get on in the world; we are to make a new contract with the other man while we do nothing for the man to whom I have referred.
In the absence of any evidence to show how many there are, I would like to have some particulars, perhaps in the form of a schedule -I do not care about the names, they can be numbered 1, 2, and so on-which would show what number are involved. One man went to work last year and one the year before, and I should like to know what is going to be done about them. Three men came in during last three years; is one man to get an increase of pay for nine years, another man for one year, another for two years and another for three years; is that the idea?
