We are going to make a new contract to increase the pay of a man who went to work in 1920 regardless of the fact that during that nine years his meritorious service has been certified to by his superior officer according to the provisions of the Civil Service Act. The Postmaster General knows the provision of the certificate, which is, "I certify on my honour, regardless of political considerations, that this man"-giving the name-"has rendered meritorious service which entitles him to receive this added pay." Those certificates exist with relation .to a large number of the men, but I want to know how many. We cannot follow what is involved in this resolution unless we have some idea of what it means with respect to individuals and pay. The Postmaster General says that the sum involved is small and that the proper place to discuss this resolution is in committee, on the bill, but once we give a second reading to the bill we have committed ourselves to the principle of it, and that principle is the payment of a sum of money. I want to know how much money the treasury will have to pay to carry out a new contract which will be made by the Dominion of Canada with ninety-six of its employees.
Every service for the state is either by an implied or by an express contract. In an express contract the terms are mentioned; in an implied contract one is enabled to recover on a quantum meruit. We had an illustration of that in connection with a dredging contract with the Public Works department under which certain services were rendered. It was said that the classification was entirely different 
from that under which the tender had been made and therefore that the contractor was entitled to a further sum of money because of the services rendered. We are now making a new contract on a quantum where there is an express contract outstanding, and I should like to know under what principle we are justified in making that new contract. I should like to have these particulars from the Postmaster General before I give my further assent on division to this resolution going up.

speechtext: Then he got the pay of his grade.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
No, that is the point.
He did not get the pay of his grade. The official grade that he occupied was that of postal helper, no matter what he was doing. I know of one case where a man who was an ex-striker had supervision over four or five other persons, all of whom were getting higher salaries than he was, but he was graded as a postal helper because that was the only grade into which he could be admitted.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That supervisory position
must have been classified somewhere under the act.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
No. He was doing the
work of a supervisee but his official grade under the civil service appointment was that of postal helper.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
If he is classified, he should
get the salary of his classification.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He was graded as a postal helper, but he might be doing all sorts of work demanding higher qualifications.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Take a clerk who is classified as a mail clerk. He arrives at the point where he may be supervising five or six other clerks under him, and yet he does not get the salary of a supervising clerk. He is placing himself in a position where he may be promoted to the position of supervising clerk. While that is the name of the position he is occupying, he has not the salary of a supervising clerk.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that
he may be classified as a supervising clerk. He does not say he was.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
He has the opportunity
of promotion to that position.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
What I am trying to get
at is this. The strike was in 1919. A man who has been out of the service for nine years goes back. In that time, might he not have so completely forgotten the work that he would have to start in the same position as a beginner?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I have a case in point,
that of a man going into the service in 1926. There was a vacancy for the position of clerk. This man passed the examination and had the qualifications just the same as the position called for in 1919. He classified for the position by passing the examination. That was Samuel Woolson. He was receiving 81,630 before, and is now receiving $1,320.

Western Postal Employees

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Receiving a salary of $1,-
320 with what classification? Is that the salary of the position for which 'he passed the examination?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes, it is in this case.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: What is he going to get out of this fund?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: $1,336. But he has been in now going on four years. The minimum since he went out has been increased in that lower class.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: In 1926 there was a vacancy in the Winnipeg post office. It was advertised. Among the applicants for that position was one who seven years before had been employed in the post office, namely, in 1919. He was awarded the .position, and now he is going to be given by this parliament $1,336. At the same time there was another vacancy, which was filled by another applicant who had not formerly been employed in the post office service. That applicant has received! his statutory increases, but will get nothing more.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He is not in such a high grade.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is exactly what we ask the minister. He has given the name of the man. What work was he doing?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Mail clerk.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: What was the other man? There were other vacancies for mail clerks in 1926.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I do not see any.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: There were in other parts of the country-we will put it that way. Then we say, because a man seven years ago worked at a job in the post office, he is now 'to get $1,300 out of the people of Canada by reason of the fact that seven years ago when he was working he went on strike. That is what parliament is doing.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: If he is capable of doing the same work that he was doing in 1919, why should he not be so paid?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: But he .passed the examination. The Civil Service have given him his rating, in accordance with the examination on the application for the job.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: As postal helper. That was the only thing he could get.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: As mail clerk in the post office.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Pardon me. Will the
minister say what salary he got?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I have this man's name here.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Sit down.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I think the house will quite agree that I must look to the minister for this information, much as I should like to get assistance from my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre. Coming events may cast their shadows behind, not before.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I might say to my hon. friend that while this is quite complicated,-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: It is not complicated.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: -I cannot see that he is making any point, comparing this man coming in with his previous experience of eight or nine years in the service with the new man coming in under examination, because no new man comes in under a grade of that kind. He must come in as a postal helper, and consequently can only be graded as such. He begins at the bottom of the ladder and works up, whereas the other man has to pass an examination as to whether he is fit for the class he was in before. But 'he does not get the salary of that class. He gets four hundred dollars less.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: We are not going to take generalities, but actualities. We are going to take this ease of 1928. The man's name was?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Samuel Woolson.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: There was a vacant position, I understand, and he applied for it. Did he write on the examination?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Thank you.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Having written on the examination, he was appointed to the position was he?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Wait a minute.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
He was appointed at the
minimum salary of $1,080.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
But what examination
did he pass?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He passed the examination for postal clerk, because they put him at that work.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is not the point.
What examination did he pass?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
The civil service examination.
Western Postal Employees

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Exactly. The same as any other applicant for a position in the service?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: The only difference was the age limit.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes. What position was advertised ?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Postal clerk-no, postal helper.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Were there several applicants?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: \\ e will have to know. We are going to get down to the reason. The Prime Minister was not in when I began to deal with this case.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
There would be several
applicants.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Seven years after the
strike there was a vacancy. It was advertised. One of the applicants was Samuel Woolson, one of the striking employees of 1919. To him the position was awarded. He received $1,080 as a starter. That was the salary stated in the advertisement for the class of position vacant when the civil service asked for applicants. According to the minister, that man in this year of grace, 1928, will receive some $1,300; whereas any other person that passed the same examination, and might have been appointed to the same position, would get nothing but the statutory increase. In other words, seven years ago, Woolson had experience, now he has none.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Oh, yes, he has.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He had seven years of no experience.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He had seven years without experience.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Without working. It does not follow that he would have forgotten all his past experience.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He had seven years in which he had not worked as a postal clerk.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? If he drops out of legal practice for seven years is he going to forget all his law?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I know some gentlemen who are very emphatic in saying that in much less than seven years a man forgets a great deal of his legal education. I think most 	f
lawyers will say that if thej' retired from the practice of law for seven years they would not care to resume it without a good deal of study.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Would not such a man be better than a law student?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes, but not as good as a new student at law.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Would he charge less for his services?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He might and he might not. It has been published in the newspapers in Winnipeg that 20 per cent of this sum is going to the lawyers.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is the trade union rate.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Among lawyers?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I am bound to say that has not been my experience. I would be much better off if it had been. Let me proceed. I trust the minister realizes where this leads to. A given number of men all pass the same examination. One, because seven years ago he was at that job, is a little more proficient in it than somebody else.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Therefore worth more.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: And, my hon. frend saj's, therefore worth more. The notice was posted up showing what the salary would be. His contract with the civil service was, just as the minister mentioned, $1,0S0. Now this parliament is going to make a new contract and give that man $1,300; but, the man who went into similar service in some other part of Canada, a man who was not a striker, a man of as good education as Woolson, is not going to get anything extra.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
My hon. friend is losing
sight of the fact that, although Woolson passed the examination and went in at the minimum salary of $1,080, he was not put to do the work of that class, but the work of a postal clerk. His experience before the strike qualified him for that higher grade and although, as the agreement said, he had to go in as a beginner, he took the examination and went in at $1,080 a year. But knowing that he was classified for this higher grade they put him to do that work although he did not receive the salary of the higher grade. And he has continued to do such work during the last four and a half years. That is how the difference is made up as between the work he did and the salary he got.

Western Postal Employees

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes; but when the minister says he did the work he must go further than that. Now, Sam Wool son reported for duty. What did he do?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: They put him in as a clerk and-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: What did he start at?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: He started as a postal helper; he graded as a postal helper.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
WThen he reported for
duty what did he do?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
He started on sortation
work and that is one of the important duties But he did not get paid at all for sortation work.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Does the minister say
that of his own knowledge-that that man started sorting the day he went to work?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I do not say it of my own knowledge but from information given me by the officials.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Does the record show
that?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I do not know whether it
does or not.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Then the minister must not say that, because he is assuming a case which the record does not show. That is why I have asked the minister with reference to this particular case, which is in point. Sam Woolson answered the advertisement. The salary was $1,080. Sam went to work at that salary of $1,080 and then he received the statutory increases. The minister says the postmaster put him at other work than that which ordinarily a clerk would do. Well, I want to know what he reported for; what he did; when he was changed; in other words, I want the history of that man's job up to this year; because it is proposed to give him $1,300, more than that given the man who stood at the desk beside him and who came in the same day.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That man did not stand
at the desk beside him but in a lower class or grade.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: What evidence have you of that?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
He was not entitled to
stand at that desk.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Once more the minister
is building a case on what he says should be. I want to know what is.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I will tell you what is:
A man going in entirely new could not stand beside this man who, although going in anew, carried with him his past experience. They were in different classes, working in different sections of the building.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
But the minister has no
evidence; he is speaking of what is going to be.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is what took place,
and I know it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
We can easily send a
telegram and satisfy the minister. The minister's story is that Sam Woolson, in response to an advertisement by the Civil Service Commission, passed an examination successfully and was awarded a position in the Winnipeg post office. Is that right?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
What was the position,
may I ask, to which Sam Woolson was appointed?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
To be positively sure we
should have to look at the record.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Of course, and that is
what I want to know; because it makes all the difference in the world. What did Sam do when he went to work?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
From what I see in the
record he would start on sortation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
This is really so important that the facts should be before us. Before the house resumed the minister showed me the documents containing the list of these employees and I had just time enough to look down the page. However, I have taken one case, in 1926, and I am now asking to what work this man was put after he was appointed to the position. The minister says he reported for duty bult he cannot be certain what the man went to work to do. I want to know:	What did he do when he reported?
How long did he remain in that position? What did 'he next do? When was he appointed to a different position? When did he attain to the position which the minister says, had he never left the service, would have enabled him to receive $1,300-more thian someone else is getting. These are the questions I should like to have answered! and I do not think they will be considered unfair.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of
what happened in Winnipeg, but to my misfortune I do know something of the rules and regulations of the Civil Service Commission, and I know that no man may enter the employ of the Post Office Department how except
Western Postal Employees

as a postal helper. In the old days there were examinations for mail clerks and clerks grade 1, grade 2, grade 3 and so forth-examinations open to the public. At the present time these examinations are open only to those who wish to apply for the position of postal helper. Consequently every one of these men, as he returned to the employ of the Post Office Department, became a postal helper; he answered the advertisement for the position of postal helper, carrying a salary of $1,080. As these men entered the post office it was found by the postmaster or by their superior officers that they might, with advtantage and with a view to efficient service, be placed in one of the higher grades, say that of mail clerk, sortation clerk, clerk of grade 1, 2 or 3, and so forth, to none of which positions they could apply through the Civil Service Commission by examination; they had to go in by the lowest grade, so to speak. So that when their superior officers found that they could actually do that work- if the information I have gathered from this discussion is correct-they were placed' in these positions-let us say in the position of sortation clerk which would carry with it a salary of say $1,500 or $1,600. So that for the past three or four years, as the case may be, these men although they entered the service at $1,080, with whatever statutory increases they received, presumably $60, have been doing work which under other circumstances would be carried on by men earning $1,600. And the purpose of this bill, if my information is correct, is to give to every such man the salary which he actually earned. My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) made that argument this afternoon, the argument based on the quantum meruit, and if I may say so quite frankly to him and to the Postmaster General, that is the only argument that is worth anything in this case; any appeals to sympathy for these men is to my mind hardly worth considering. But I wish to direct the attention of the Committee to this point: that the resolution does not seem to say just what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the Postmaster General have in mind. The resolution states:
That it is expedient to provide for the readjustment of the salaries of certain postal employees in western Canada who were dismissed in 1919 and subsequently re-employed, to give them the benefit of salary they would have received had they re-entered the service in the class equivalent to the one they were in when dismissed.
I do not favour that proposition at all. As I understand it, the proposition made by the Postmaster General and laid down by the

hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was to pay the men for the work they have actually done during that time and not to pay them on the basis of the salary they might have received had they gone back and done that work. For instance, the case was put to us to-day of one man who had been earning $1,800 before the strike. He went on strike and came back, starting at say $1,080. If that man was doing $1,800 worth of work I am prepared to pay him accordingly, but I am not prepared to say that we should give him the equivalent of his salary when he went on strike. I am not prepared to give him that money unless it can be shown to the satisfaction of the Postmaster General and of the officers of the department that he actually was doing work which under other circumstances would have given him this money. I should not be prepared to go even so far.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman think that a big favour is done these men to take them back at all?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is the point I was
coming to. In the first place, I am not sure that I should ever have taken them back. But now that we have taken them back we cannot forever keep hanging over their heads as a punishment this prospect: "You may work as hard as you please, and give the best service you can to the country, but because you made that one fatal mistake we shall never reward you for your efforts."

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is exactly the
attitude we take.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I want to get this clear.
If I understand my hon. friend's attitude now it is that for the rest of their lives these men must be punished for the action they took in 1919.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No, our attitude is exactly the same as that taken by my hon. friend, that from this day on we will make the past something to be forgotten and pay them for the work they are doing.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Then we are not so far
apart after all in principle; there is very little difference between us. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that from to-day everything is to be forgotten and that these men will be paid the salary actually earned at the work they are actually doing now.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Yes, that is it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
My hon. friends agree that from to-day we should pay these men the salaries which are carried by the positions

Western Postal Employees
they are actually occupying; that is to say, though they may have gone in as postal helpers last year and immediately become sortation clerks because they were able to do that work, from to-day we should start to pay those men $200 or $300 more.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is my understanding.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Then the only difference
between us is that hon. gentlemen opposite are starting a year later than we on this side. The same principle applies and it is only a question of quantum.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
There is this difference
in principle: We take the attitude that the man who started last year was, as my hon. friend admitted, lucky to be taken back at all in view of the fact that he went out on a sympathetic strike. From the time he began again until the present he has received perhaps a lower salary than he was really earning according to the work he was doing, but that was his punishment for going out on that strike. From to-day on we say "Let bygones be bygones, and we will pay you for the work you are doing, as certified by the postmaster.'

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: So the principle is this, that in 1920 the government of the day, out of the goodness of its heart and not because there was an election coming on, which would not have been fair; out of the kindness of its heart in 1920, a year before the election of 1921, the government said to these men, "Come back; all is forgiven."

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
The strike occurred only
two years before that; we could not do it very much sooner.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Probably that is quite right, but nine years later the members of that same party say, "If you come back you must put in one whole year without getting the salary wnicn you earn." Supposing a man comes back to-morrow, after we pass this bill, where are we going to put him? Are we to put him to work as a sortation clerk and give him $200 a year extra because he happens to come back the day after this bill is passed?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not
stated the position quite correctly. The government of that day said, "We will take you back on certain conditions" and those conditions have been lived up to by the government. We think those conditions should continue to apply.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the
conditions except from what I heard this afternoon. I understand that these men were to be taken back subject to certain conditions, 78594-144
which simply amounted to the men saying they were very sorry and would not do it again. Another condition, which was in their favour, was to the effect that these men, going up for their examinations, need not be within the age limit. Those were the only two conditions I heard mentioned.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
And they retained their
pension and superannuation rights.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is correct, but there
was no condition as to what their salaries should be and I submit that for us to come before this country to-day and say "We forgave you nine years ago but to-day we are not going to pay you the salary you earn" is a ridiculous position to take.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I am sorry my hon.
friend from Quebec South has not followed the debate as carefully as he usually does. The four conditions mentioned by the Postmaster General this afternoon, which were referred to in the order in council which permitted the old employees to be re-employed -not reinstated-were first the approval of the governor in council; secondly, the passing of that examination, waiving the age limit, and thirdly, the fact that these men came to the department as new employees and, coming as such they received the pay payable to new employees. That was the contract, and now we are substituting a parliamentary contract for the one which was made between the state and the individual.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
They were to receive the
pay of new employees while they were doing the work of new employees.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I am coming to that.
My hon. friend at once took the point which, as a lawyer. I expected he would take; he submitted that to put forth the principle mentioned in that resolution would be destructive of the civil service of Canada. There is no question about that; the hon. gentleman saw that point at once, but he said he was in favour of every man being paid what he was worth. Once more we are left in the cloudland of conjecture and doubt as to who is to determine what a man's worth may be.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That should be determined
by the work he does.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Exactly, and it was because of that point that I endeavoured to extract from the Postmaster General the information I am now trying to secure. I took the Woolson case because I thought it might be typical. Let it be observed first that these

Western Postal Employees

men come in as though they were unknown to the state; they make application in response to an advertisement issued by the Civil Service Commission. We will say three men apply, and we might designate them as A, B and C, B having been employed in the Winnipeg post office seven years previously. They write their examinations and B gets the position; he is appointed to the position called for by the advertisement, as the hon. member for Quebec South admitted.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
There is only one position,
that of postal helper.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Exactly. B gets that
position, and having been appointed to that position he cannot be promoted at once; that is a matter for the Civil Service Commission and the Post Office Department, through its officials. As I pointed1 out this afternoon, when a competent superior officer reports that this employee has performed meritorious service entitling him to a raise in pay, he receives the statutory increase and therefore obtains added compensation.
Now, every man in a post office who is a helper is looking forward to doing something better, and the postmaster tries him at another job just a little better than the one he previously held. According to the argument now being advanced and the principle favoured, we are to say hereafter that if during the year the postmaster of a post office puts a man at a little different job from that for which' he was hired under the Civil Service Commission, that man is going to ask for more pay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: If the position carries it.	[DOT]

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Every job which is a
little better than the job formerly held by a man carries with it a little higher pay; that is why men strive to obtain better jobs. That is the reason the ambitious man is always willing to try his hand at a little more difficult task, in order ultimately to obtain a little more pay.
i_r. POWER: But there is a vast difference between a man who has obtained a position as postal helper and a man who is a sortation clerk, we will say. There is a difference in salary of perhaps $600, and if it is true that some of these men were brought in as postal helpers and immediately made to do sortation work I think they should be paid accordingly.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is the information I have been trying to secure from the Postmaster General. I am advised that not a man was told to do anything which he formerly did after he went back to work as a postal helper; later, having worked as a postal helper, he got another job because he was better fitted for it or because he was more ambitious. I will say this; a young, ambitious man of twenty-five, making up his mind to get on-and remember, they waived the age limit-is going to get on to the next job as quickly as the man who has been out of the service for seven years, if not more quickly. 1 know the observation of my hon. friend will be that that is the reason there is an age limit.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
What may have happened
and what is likely to have happened is that the postmaster or the superior officer at Winnipeg took the older man who had been out seven years and gave him the higher position, or rather gave him the more important work to do.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Let us ask ourselves this question:	What benefits have been conferred
upon the striking employee, apart from the financial benefits sought to be given to him? First, the age limit was withdrawn, and that was a tremendous concession. What is the second concession? He still has bis rights under the superannuation and pensions acts. He is deprived of his claim to seniority because you cannot overcome time and say that a man who went to work in 1625 is going to rank senior to a man who went to work in 1918; that is one of the things he is deprived of. What else is he deprived of? Nothing. He comes in as a new employee and he carries with his position the salary of a new employee, but if he does-and this is where it is so essential to get an answer from the Postmaster General-work of a higher class, which carried with it in the days gone by a higher pa}', * he shall be treated as though there had been continuity in his service, notwithstanding that he is seven years older and has been out during that time.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is the resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is the resolution,
yes. That is the resolution which I understand the hon. gentleman says he cannot give his support to. There is no play of words about this. May I say to the right hon. the Prime Minister that in one instance he is being

Western Postal Employees
compensated as though there were continuity of service and in the other instance there is the statement made, as the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has said, "I want this man paid for the class of work he does."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is all
the government want; that is our understanding of the resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Assuming that that is
what the government want to do then I submit that that is not what the resolution says. Leaving that for the moment, the difference between us seems to be very simple. We are willing to have the Post Office Department consider it in .the light of service rendered but not make it retroactive; the government desire to make it retroactive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: If he has been employed right along.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
As the hon. member for
Quebec South has pointed out, the question is:	How are we going to determine with
exactness that the man did the work of a higher class? I saw the Postmaster General's schedule and all he does to arrive at the sum is this:
Appointment: at such and such a time.
Salary: such and such an amount.
Salary when he left the service seven years ago: so much.
Amount received during the years he has been employed: so much.
Amount he would have received had he continued on at the pay he was getting when he left: so much.
Difference he is entitled to: so much, less adj ustments.
As I understand the right hon. the Prime Minister and .the member for Quebec South, that is exactly what we do not want to do.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Wre do not want that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
In fairness to the other
employees there is only one way in which it can be dealt with, and that is not to make it retroactive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
There has been a discussion as to the principles which should govern in this matter. The first principle mentioned was that underlying reinstatement, and the second was the principle underlying remuneration. We on this side of the house say that the application of the principle of reinstatement was settled by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in office; -that the principle of reinstatement as being applicable was settled at the time of the strike. The question of whether or not the men should 78594-144J
be taken back after the strike was decided by the government of the day. The government of the day did not decide that question of reinstatement in the manner in which we are attempting to decide the present one of remuneration, namely by an act of parliament, but decided it by an order in council under the War Measures Act. I have nothing to say about t'heir method of procedure beyond observing that I do not think it was right; the government apparently took advantage of the act to say that these men were to be reinstated. When the government took that position they made it perfectly plain that they were prepared to reinstate the men notwithstanding the part they had taken in the strike.
In order to obtain any position the men had to pass a civil service examination which admitted them only to the lowest position in the service. They were admitted to the service in that manner, but, having been admitted, they were, in view of acquired skill and previous training, given work which required a degree of experience and skill very much greater than that to which the examination related and which would have been required of men going into the service for the first time. We say that these men where they have been put into positions requiring a greater degree of skill and experience should be paid for the service which they are or have been rendering, notwithstanding the fact that they agreed to come back as though they were entering the service for the first time. In other words, the principle governing remuneration is that of paying what the service rendered is worth. I am prepared to leave to the government of the day the question as to whether the men should have been reinstated or not. That question was settled in 1920, but once men enter the government service then I say that there is only one principle which should govern in. the matter of remuneration, and that is the value of the service which is being rendered. If these men are performing services which are worth more than they are being paid and which they would be receiving but for having participated in the strike, if they are filling positions which carry higher salaries than those which they are receiving, then I think they should be given the difference between what they are being paid and what they would have been paid for the particular class of work they are or have been performing. As I understand it, that is the purpose of the bill based on .the present resolution. If the measure goes farther than that, if it attempts to pay to any man an additional sum of money, notwithstanding-the fact that the work which he
Western Postal Employees

has been performing does not carry that salary, then I am with my hon. friends opposite in agreeing that such an amount should not be paid.
If hon. members will pardon me, as evidencing that what I am now saying is not a newly formed conviction, I should like to refer to a statement of principle in matters of remuneration, as I had stated it before this strike ever took place, and which appears in a volume entitled Industry and Humanity, published in 1918, which volume is a study in the principles underlying industrial reconstruction. It appears in a chapter entitled Principles Underlying Work, at page 272 of the volume, and is as follows:
What labour is really concerned about as regards remuneration, is adequate reward of the effort put forth. What capital and management are really concerned about is adequate reward for their investments and services. What the community is really concerned about is adequate value in services and commodities for purchasing power. The method of remuneration qf labour which helps most to secure adequacy of returns all round is the method which is likely to prove the most productive of efficiency, and, in the long run, the most advantageous to labour.
What is earned, rather than what is received, or paid, is the fundamental consideration. Men should get what they earn, and should earn what they get.
As I understand it, that is the whoLe principle underlying the present resolution. What is earned, rather than what is received or paid, is the fundamental consideration on the part of labour, and that principle should govern, particularly in the matter of government employment. Once these men came back into the employ of the state they should have been paid what their services were worth, in other words, the amounts corresponding to the classification in which their services fall. If they are performing the services of sorters they should be paid the wages which are due to sorters, not the wages which would be paid to men in the lower grades. That is the whole purpose of this measure.
I think the purpose of both sides of the house is much the same. Our purpose certainly is the same as that which actuated hon. gentlemen opposite when they passed the order in council to permit these men to return to the service. It is that of bringing about industrial peace, and industrial peace cannot be brought about effectively so long as you leave a sense of injustice rankling in the mind of any man as to the terms of his employment and the service he is rendering to the community and his employer. Hon. gentlemen opposite thought that they were helping the cause of industrial peace, when, under the War Measures Act, they passed an order

in council permitting men, who had participated in a very serious strike, to return to the service of the state on certain terms and conditions. We feel -that in so doing they went a considerable length towards restoring and maintaining industral peace, not only as concerns the few individuals most affected, but as affecting labour generally throughout the country. But since that time, ten years have gone by; certain men in the post office at Winnipeg have been rendering specific services to the state, and during all that time those of their number who went out on strike in 1910 have been receiving less pay than they would otherwise have received for the services which they have been rendering. We say that so long as that is continued, a sense of injustice will remain. Hon. gentlemen opposite meet us in this way; they say: we will agree with you and we will discontinue that discrimination to-night 'because we believe that it is an injustice. If that is true tonight, it was equally true a year ago, two years ago. It was equally true as each man began to perform a service that is worth more than he was being paid for. We ask that that sense of injustice shall be removed so that not only this particular group of men but labour generally, may feel that the government of the country as an employer, is not seeking to profit by the necessity of any man, whether the necessity arises out of a particular part taken in an industrial dispute or otherwise.
Once the question of a dispute is settled and reinstatement is permitted, the. state as a model employer, should be prepared to pay and allow payment of the remuneration whibh properly attaches to particular positions. That is as far as the government is prepared to go in sanctioning the resolution before the house. It is our understanding of the bill to be based on tihe resolution, and if in any particular the resolution goes further than that, it might as well be made apparent at the moment that the government will not sanction the introduction of any bill which goes beyond that point. That far we feel we should go. We believe hon. gentlemen in what they have said to-day are somewhat of that opinion in view of the change of feeling that has come with the passing of time. We, at all events, have come to the conclusion that if men have suffered a severe measure of punishment through eight or ten years of suspense as to what would be their future lot, in losing throughout that time the opportunity to invest the little moneys they might otherwise have received, and in the permanent loss of their seniority rights, we, as a government seeking to bring about, so far as

Western Postal Employees
possible, good will in all relations, international and industrial, can well afford to go the length this resolution goes to-night.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has used a word- and I cannot but think he h'as done it unintentionally-which is exactly a negation of the fact. He used the word, "reinstated." The older in council does not reinstate anyone. That is the whole trouble. The order in council permits reemployment, but it reinstates no one and yet during his speech my right hon. friend used the word, "reinstatement" continuously. Reinstatement means just what its derivation is -put him back in the state in which he was. This order in council permitted' no such thing. It said distinctly, first, your employment has been terminated1; second, you went out on a sympathetic strike and that terminated your employment, and, third, you now admit that you are conscious of the gravity of the offence that ylou committed against the State. You are now allowed to be re-employed in the public service although the1 original order in council debarred you from re-employment in any capacity. There never was a question of reinstatement. It has never even been suggested that there should be reinstatement. The word is forgotten. The proper word is "re-employment", and re-employment was predicated upon conforming to certain conditions. Those conditions were enumerated this afternoon and I will not repeat them. But when the applicant for a position complied with those conditions he had a position. That position was under a contract between him and the state. It was no longer a matter of implication; it was a matter of exact and express contract. There is no clearer rule than this: that toe terms of an express contract between parties govern and no extraneous matters can be introduced to vary, alter or change the terms of that contract unless under certain circumstances which do not exist in this case. Therefore we have an express contract of employment at a given salary. The resolution before the house supports a principle that the Prime Minister says he is not in favour of, but which in terms states that if the re-employed, discharged employees were employed in a given capacity before the strike they shall, when re-employed, receive the salary of that, position regardless of the fact that they did the work of their former jobs continuously or only part time. In other words, the money that is to be paid is predicated upon what they received and what they would have received.

They would be paid only
for the number of days, weeks, months or years that they worked.

That is not what the
resolution says and not what those figures show. The hon. gentleman showed me a sheet of paper and it gives the date of appointment with the salary at that date. Then it gives the man's former salary, whalt he received during the time he was employed and what he would have received if there had been no break in his service. One is deducted from ;the other and that is what he is entitled, subject to some adjustments, to receive. That is not what the Prime Minister said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I must thank my hon. friend for suggesting that perhaps I had not made myself clear, or rather had expressed what was not in my mind when I drew a distinction between reinstatement and re-employment. When I referred to reinstatement I was referring to a man going back to work in the place in which he had been previously engaged. I meant that he was going back to his former work-'the word is derived from the Latin "status" meaning place -that is, he was going back into his place when he was going back into the position of a postal employee. That was settled by hon. gentlemen opposite when they passed their order in council. But I will drop the word "reinstatement" altogether. I will speak only of re-employment.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is toe word.
