maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: My hon. friend says, "that is the word." We will stick to that. Hon. gentlemen opposite and not this government decided that certain men were to be re-employed.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No, might be.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Well, might be, and the largest number of them were re-employed by hon. gentlemen opposite by an order in council which they put through. At any rate they settled the principle that men who had been out on strike could be re-employed in the postal service of Can-
Western Postal Employees

ada. We are in agreement in regard to the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite settled the principle of re-employment. Now comes the question as to the basis of re-employment, the principle that shall govern in matters of re-employment. This is where the difference comes in. We on this side of the house say that if these men are to be employed, the principle which shall govern in the matter of remuneration is that of services rendered, and that that principle alone should govern. We say that no government has any right to mate contracts with men to perform services and to pay a less amount than is normally paid for those services in accordance with the general regulations of the department by which they are employed. Hon. gentlemen opposite want these men who are re-employed to be paid at a lower rate than their particular employment is recognized as commanding. We say that is contrary to the whole practice of maintaining a standard of wages as followed by employers throughout the country generally. We say that a certain quantity of labour and a certain quality of labour should carry a certain remuneration, and what we propose by this measure is to say that men who were reemployed under an order in council which hon. gentlemen opposite passed shall be paid now as though they had been re-employed on terms which would admit them to receive as remuneration the amounts of money which attach to the particular classes of work they were doing; not to go any further than that. May I make it clear to my hon. friends that if the resolution of the Postmaster General means anything more than that, the government will not sanction his bringing in, and will not ask this house to pass, any bill which goes further than that. If the bill which my hon. friend the Postmaster General introduces is not specific enough in its terms, we can amend it. The intention of the government is simply to fix the method of remuneration and the amount of remuneration in accordance with that attaching to the classes of work actually performed, letting bygones be bygones in the case of remuneration just as hon. gentlemen opposite did in the matter of reemployment.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is my understanding of the effect of the resolution. If it meant anything else I never would have introduced it. Let me say here that the difference between these salaries is based on the nature of the work performed, and that would be determined by the reports throughout the number of years made by the office at Winnipeg. No fairer way could be adopted than taking the 
weekly and monthly and quarterly reports, the yearly reports, if you like, together with the case examinations of all these officials in the different classes or grades they occupy, and basing the remuneration upon those reports according to the class of work performed.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has
mentioned a number of times the order in council and the principle we established in passing it; I mean the government of 1920, of which I was not a member. I hold the order in council in my hand. It was loaned to me by the Postmaster General. I am going to read two or three clauses that are pertinent, and if hon. gentlemen desire it, I will read it all, although it is somewhat lengthy. I do not agree with the Prime Minister that we established the principle of taking these men back and giving them remuneration equal to that which they were previously receiving, for that is what the Prime Minister implied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No, I say you did not do that, but that you should have done so. That is where you made your mistake. You either should have said: these men will not be re-employed; we cannot sanction the principle of re-employing men who go out on strike in a great public service like the postal service; or you should have said: there are circumstances which permit their re-employment. Then if you re-employed them you should have said: we will re-employ them on the basis of paying them for the actual services performed.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
We did not need to take a hard and fast position. We can occasionally take the middle road, just as my right hon. friend the Prime Minister does frequently, and I am not criticising him for that. In 1920 the government of that day took what I consider was the middle of the road. Let me quote from the order in council, dated June 4 1920. It says in respect to taking on these men:
In accordance with the understanding arrived at by the government, as embodied in a memorandum forwarded to the Civil Service Commission by Senator Robertson on the 7th January, 1920, ex-postal employees are to be considered eligible for appointment to positions in the civil service, subject to certain conditions therein mentioned.
Then on the other side is the memorandum giving the canditions. Again I will quote the pertinent clauses:
The gravity of their offence against the state being now realized, the government has given consideration to the possibility of removing the bar to their application through the Civil Service Commission for re-employment in the public service, and His Excellency the Governor

Western Postal Employees
in Council is disposed to exercise clemency so far as reasonably consistent with necessary discipline.
Ex-postal employees may therefore be considered as eligible to be appointed to positions in the civil service for which they make application as vacancies occur, and to which, in the opinion of the commission, they are justly entitled under the regulations.
All right; they were appointed to the positions for which they made application. That is all the government of 1920 agreed to, to re-appoint them to the positions for which they made application. These men, I understand after listening to the debate, applied to be appointed as postal helpers.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Under the regulation they could not apply for anything else.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
The agreement distinctly
states that they would be appointed to the positions for which they made application.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
My hon. friend misses
the significance of the words he has just read -" under the regulations." The regulations would not permit them to apply for any other position.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
I cannot help that. They applied for the position of postal helper. The order in council with the memorandum attached says that they may be appointed as vacancies occur to positions to which in the opinion of the Civil Service Commission they are justly entitled under the regulations. The Civil Service Commission considered that they were entitled to be appointed as postal helpers, and they were appointed as such, and they received the pay of postal helpers. It is true that some of them-I would not say all of them-did work of a higher grade, just as in ordinary business, as the leader of the opposition has pointed out, you will find one out of three or four men in the same concern who is much more able and does much more work and better work than the others, although all are getting exactly the same pay. Some of these men, having had previous experience, may have done a better class of work.
So far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we are ready to let bygones be bygones. We say that probably these men have received sufficient punishment, and that in the future we are willing that they should receive the wages attached to the positions for which they are certified.
The Prime Minister made another point. Reading from his own book he enunciated the axiom that men should get paid for the work they do. We all agree with that, but he was not dealing in his book just at that point with men who had' gone on strike from
a great public service. He was merely speaking in general.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I was dealing with the principles underlying industrial peace.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
He was not dealing with
men who had gone on strike from the public service. I do not know the context of the passage quoted, but at any rate it seems to me that the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house lives up entirely to the order in council of 1920, which was passed, as was expressly stated, as an act of clemency. We take the position now, that for the sake of national unity and harmony in this country in the future these men should receive the wages of the positions for which they are fitted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
May I say
just a word about the order in council which my hon. friend has just read? I asked the hon. leader of the opposition this afternoon just where the authority came from to pass that particular order in council. We have heard a good deal in parliament this session about the powers given by parliament to the Civil Service Commission. The law governing employment in the civil service states that civil servants of the class we are considering, must receive their employment through the Civil Service Commission under the terms which the commission lays down. These men were not re-employed under the terms of the Civil Service Act. That was the first breach. If hon. gentlemen had been concerned about the observance and enforcement of the Civil Service Act and what it demanded of an administration, not one of these men could have been taken back under the terms of the order in council.
May I say further that the Civil Service Commission to-day or any other day would not think of bargaining with men to go into the public service and to accept work there on lower terms than the standards which govern in the particular classes of employment for which they were to be engaged. We might well realize at this time that what parliament is now passing upon is the principle of what men shall be paid for services rendered. Parliament was not passing on that particular principle when this order in council was passed. The government of the day was then laying down certain conditions with regard to re-employing certain public servants. My own view is that these men should never have been re-employed except by act of parliament; that proceeding under the War Measures Act and in disregard of the Civil Service Act was not a correct method of
Western Postal Employees

procedure but, certain former employees having been re-employed, parliament is now asked to say on what basis of remuneration they shall be paid. Shall they be paid a rate of remuneration in accordance with the services they have actually rendered, or shall there be some compromise in tha-t particular? In the matter of remuneration I submit that parliament cannot take any other ground than that of paying men for the actual services they have rendered.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Once more the right hon. Prime Minister, I think, has either not wholly grasped the situation as it has been presented by the documents, or else he attributes a meaning to the order in council that I cannot read into it. The War Measures Act, I assumed-I said I was not certain-was the only authority for the order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is right.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Are the words "War Measures Act" contained in the order in council?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend from Rimouski, I have looked at the order in council for the first time-it is handed to me by the hon. Postmaster General-and it does not indicate on the face of it anything with regard to the War Measures Act.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: Does it indicate any parliamentary authority at all?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
No. It is merely a report. I think I had better read it. This is the order in council:
The committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 31st May 19^0 from the Secretary of State, submitting that tne Civil kerVice Commission has recently received applications for positions in the civil service from ex-postal employees who participated m the sympathetic strike in western Canada in the spring of 1919.
In accordance with the understanding arrived at by the government, as embodied in a memorandum forwarded to the Civil Service Commission by Senator Robertson on the 7th January, 1920,_ ex-postal employees are to be considered eligible for appointment to positions m the civil service, subject to certain conditions therein mentioned.
The ex-postal employees mentioned in the attached list have complied with the conditions or this memorandum.
The minister, therefore, recommends that authority be granted for the appointment of these candidates to positions for which they are eligible.
The committee advise that the requisite authority be granted accordingly.
(Signed) Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council. IMr. Mackenzie King.]
The memorandum my hon. friend from Fort William has just read. The Postmaster General read it this afternoon. But may I point out, I cannot think the right hon. Prime Minister intends to go as far as his observation would lead one to conclude. The state has never been able, nor has any private employer, ever been able to calculate-shall I say?-the kilowatts of work that the human machine can render in any particular place. I recall the general manager of one of the great banks of this country endeavoured to determine the capacity of each of the employees by fixing a standard that would be the measure of his work. If he exceeded that standard, then he was ranked accordingly; and if he fell below that standard he usually sought other employment. Now, we cannot do that with respect to each individual in the post office. That is clear is it not?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No, we actually do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: It is done by the classification in the civil service.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is in the mass. That is just the point I am making. Being unable to determine what each individual may render in the way of quantum of work, we have endeavoured to classify civil servants, and the classification is arbitrary. For instance, the great railway corporations have schedules classifying their employees according to the work they do. Those schedules cover section foremen, machinists, engineers, firemen, conductors, brakemen, wipers, hostlers, and so on. In this case we are endeavouring to correct what the Prime Minister thinks is unfairness to a group of people by arbitrarily saying: We will pay them what they would have got if they had never quit. That is wherein I say this measure-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: That is what the resolution says.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: No doubt.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
But that is not what the
Prime Minister has said, or what the member from Quebec has said. That is another point.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
It is not what the Prime Minister says at all. This resolution is the exact negation of what he says. This resolution arbitrarily says that John Smith, who in 1919 was classified as A 1 and getting SI.500 a year, and in 1925 was appointed to a position which carried with it only SI,000, can now draw at the rate of $1,500 a year from the date of appointment to his present position because when he was formerly in the service of the crown he got $1,500 a year.

Western Postal Employees
That is the resolution if English means anything. I do submit that under these circumstances perhaps the end that we all have in our minds will 'be served if this committee rise and! report progress on the resolution. I suggest to the Prime Minister that the Postmaster General take this course, so that the law officers may have an opportunity to look at the resolution and the bill to be founded on it. And, further, that the Postmaster General furnish us with a list of the employees, and the way in which they are being dealt with under the measure, so that we may be able to establish that the principle on which the government is proceeding is the principle which I have just mentioned. The principle of the measure is not what the Postmaster General now says; his figures are quite the opposite. They take an arbitrary sum that somebody received when he was dismissed, and they apply that to somebody s salary from the time that he was re-employed. It is not intended to do this at all, unless, as the Prime Minister says, Smith, we will say did that work; and there is no evidence that he did the work. As my hon. friend from Lunenberg has remarked, there should be a fact-finding commission. And that is where the principle is all wrong, because if you are going to apply it to these men you should apply it to any man who in the course of his employment is desirous of doing more work than his position calls for. No man ever got anywhere by looking at the clock and seeing how little he could do and retain his position. Men now are going to be penalized who have not done that, but have endeavoured to do something more than their duty called' for. Under these circumstances I think the only way in which the committee can ever make real headway is to rise and report progress on the resolution and ask leave to sit again. This will afford the government an opportunity to look into the measure, especially having regard to the terms of the resolution and the bill to be founded on it, so we may at least know, without endeavouring to amend the bill, what we are voting about and what principle we are giving effect to by enacting the legislation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not
wish to take up too much of the time of the house, but there seems to be a possibility of agreement in principle between those who sit on the other side of the house and those who sit on this side. The leader of the opposition referred to a memorandum by Senator Robertson, accepted by the government of the day and made the basis of the order in council which provided for the re-employment of
these men. Now, that order in council set forth two conditions only, the first being that the approval of council must be given in the case of every man who was taken back into the service; the second being that satisfactory assurances must be given that there would be no repetition of the offence. Those are the only two conditions. Then there is a third proviso which waives the age limit. There were two other conditions that became attached to the re-employment of these men by reason of the state of the law as it existed then and as it exists now. These further conditions, which are not referred to anywhere in the memorandum or the order in council, are these; first, the ex-striker must pass the ordinary civil service examination; secondly, he can come in only at the foot of the service. These two latter conditions are attached to the re-employment by reason of the fact that the Civil Service Act in itself does not provide for a situation such as this.
The leader of the opposition stated, I think quite pertinently, that it was impassible to assess the value of the persons who are in the government service. Under the conditions that were laid down in 1920 it was not possible to give recognition to the principle which the Prime Minister has enunciated and which the leader of the opposition appears to accept, namely, that employees of the government should be paid according to the value of the services they have rendered.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
Were not these conditions
punitive in their nature?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
No; the two latter conditions of which I speak followed as a natural consequence from the fact that there is no provision in the Civil Service Act for reinstatement even when an injustice has been done, or for the reemployment of a man who has left the service. I know of one case. It is known in the service here. A civil servant in Ottawa left a position in which he had attained a certain salary. He resigned in order to take a position with a firm in one of the larger cities. That firm failed. The man was desirous of returning to the position in the civil service from which he had resigned, and the authorities in the department under which he had served were desirous of obtaining his services again. Under the Civil Service Act however it was not possible for him to resume that position with the salary which he had formerly received. There were no other applicants for the position, yet he had to come in at the bottom of that particular classification. The Civil Service Act is defective in that it does not permit the application of the principle which the Prime Minister and the
Western Postal Employees

leader of the opposition are both agreed upon, and therefore it is necessary to have amended legislation to do full justice in this case.
I quite agree that it is impossible to assess in terms of money with any degree of nicety or accuracy the value of human qualities. But we have one criterion to which we might quite easily appeal in this case. Take for instance the men who were taken back in 1920 and 1921. It is not a very difficult matter to assess these men according to the value of their services to the public: in 1919 when they were in the service we recognized the value of their services by paying them a certain sum of money. That was the standard we applied to all the employees of the Dominion government. Is it not a reasonable standard to apply in this case? Is it not reasonable therefore to say that in the great majority of these cases justice will be done if we say to these men: "We will pay you as from the date of your reemployment in the service the salary which you would have received had you been taken back into the service at the same salary you were receiving when you were dismissed." That is the value which the government itself placed on services of these men prior to their dismissal, and that is the standard of value that can be applied to these men now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) has made a suggestion which, in the light of the discussion up to the present moment, is one which the committee might well consider. Before, however, the Postmaster General moves that the committee rise and report progress, I want to make tolerably sure that we are in agreement on an essential point.
I have said that so far as the government are concerned our view is that any payment to be made under the bill to be brought in must be payment for services actually rendered. That is the essence of the position we take, and it :s, I understand, on that point that my hon. friend opposite has taken exception to the resolution as drafted. When the committee resumes, the resolution will have to be amended in accordance with the line I have indicated, and I should like to ask my hon. friend whether some such amendment as the one I shall now suggest would meet the situation so far as his point is concerned. Of course,
I realize that hon. gentlemen opposite may be opposed to the resolution generally.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext: To the retroactive feature.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND RE-EMPLOYED
speechtext:
On the other
hand, there is less liability of a difference between us if we confine the resolution to payment for services actually rendered and in

accordance with what would be the recognized rate of payment for those services were there no other consideration, apart from the services themselves, to be taken into account. The resolution, then, will be somewhat to this effect:
That it is expedient to provide for the readjustment of the salaries of certain postal employees in western Canada who were dismissed in 1919 and subsequently reemployed, to give them-
And these or similar words will be inserted:
-in so far as the services performed by them will justify-
And then the words which follow in the resolution:
-the benefit of salary they would have received had they reentered the service in the class equivalent to the one they were in when dismissed, and of subsequent salary revisions.

speechtext: Without discussing the question of difference between us with respect to retroactive legislation of this kind, I maj observe that if the right hon. gentleman proposes to give effect to the contentions as he has submitted them to the committee, I think that language somewhat similar to that which he has read will entirely serve the purpose. But there is one difficulty which must be present in the right hon. gentleman's mind: How is that to be ascertained?

speechtext: We shall have to satisfy the committee on that point.

tedious, but I should like to point this out. When the applicant for the position went to work he obviously must have worked in that position which was awarded to him. When you begin to discuss that phase of the question you are met with this further difficulty: that at the end of each year recommendations were made as to the meritorious services of each employee, and when that recommendation was made the officer making it obviously considered the character of the work done and took into consideration the fact that the employee had done work which was beyond the narrow confines of the precise position to which he had been appointed. Therefore to *the extent to which his meritorious services Warranted an Increase he has already had it by recommendations made from year to year. That is a factor that must be kept in mind in dealing with this matter, and it is because of

its complexity in that regard that I have asked the minister to furnish us with particulars. Perhaps the minister in the interim will give us the schedule, adding thereto something which does not now appear in it, namely, the salaries individuals are now receiving.

speechtext:
As this is the last item in
this list I have a few words to say in connection with the unfair distribution of the
8750,000	which is to be spent on harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia. I find of that amount about $150,000 is to be expended in the constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence, which adjoins my own constituency. I have no fault to find with that; I am glad he has obtained that amount of money, but I want to call the attention of the minister to the fact that he has shown great partiality. My constituency contains more breakwaters than does the constituency of the minister, but the appropriation for the constituency of Digby-Annapolis is only $47,500 as compared with the $150,000 for the constituency of Yarmouth-Shelburne. I want to ask the minister if he thinks that is a fair distribution of the public moneys of this country. Are not the people in my constituency just as much entitled to receive appropriations in order to put their breakwaters and harbours into a condition which will permit them to earn their living as the people in the constituency of my hon. friend? He cannot go on doing business in this way and expect the people to be satisfied and not criticize the estimates.
I want to point out further that of this amount of $47,500, $33,000 is devoted to the Digby pier. This is not an appropriation for the benefit of the people in the community; it is for the benefit of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and they are paying the government 7 per cent.
Last year I brought to the attention of the minister a very much needed extension which was required to the breakwater at Westport, Nova Scotia, one of the largest fishing centres we have in the bay of Fundy. This place has more fishermen and produces more fish than does the village of Port Maitland, for which $50,000 was appropriated and another $50,000 is being asked for this year. I want to ask the minister if he thinks that is either fair or just to the fishermen of Nova Scotia, especially in view of what the government say they are trying to do for the fishing industry of tlie maritime provinces. They are spending a large portion of the public moneys

in the constituencies represented by the hon. Minister of National Defence and the member for Antigonish-Guysborough. As I said before, the constituency of Digby-Annapolis is just as important a fishing constituency as is Shelbume-Yarmouth or Antigonish-Guysborough, but the government are neglecting the public works there to the great disadvantage of the district. I wanted to call this matter to the attention of the minister before the item passed, and I hope he will see his way clear to put a sufficient amount in the supplementary estimates to cover the extension of the breakwater at Westport and the necessary dredging and repairs required for the other breakwaters in my constituency.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: There is one observation I would like to make without further trespassing upon the time of the committee. During quite a storm last summer I drove up along the coast in the county which the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis represents. I saw a large number of these breakwaters to which he has referred, and the small fishing vessels were seeking shelter behind them. The very word ''breakwater" implies the reason for their being constructed, and some of them were certainly in ill repair. It occurs to me that if we are going to protect the lives of the fishermen and expand the export business in fish-we are endeavouring to do that because if I recall correctly the exports last year were something like $34,000,000-we can only do it by keeping these breakwaters in repair. It would not take a very large sum of money to keep them in reasonable repair, and that should be done for the two reasons. The first reason is the preservation of the lives of the men who go down to the sea for the purpose of engaging in the fishing business, and the second is that they may be able to carry on their vocation under as favourable conditions as possible and thereby expand our business and carry the fish of Canada into the markets of the world. If the engineers of the department will look into this matter I am quite satisfied that they will report that many of these breakwaters should be repaired. This is a matter which should be beyond the reach of patronage; it is not a matter which the minister can deal with himself because he has to listen to what is presented to him by the ministers from the provinces and dispose of the money he is granted to the best advantage, but for the reasons I have given, I suggest that this should be beyond patronage. It is a question of life, and as far as possible the matter of safety and endeavour should be looked after by the government regardless of any other consideration. I thought I would mention this matter in view of what I saw with my own eyes last summer as I drove up along the Digby shore.

The hon. member knows that the Port Maitland breakwater constitutes practically the only safe shelter from Yarmouth up to St. Mary's bay on a very open coast where there is a great deal of fishing. When the men return to shore they meet with a difficult situation unless they have some sort of shelter, and that is why that work is being conducted.
I know it has been a long time in process, as the first length of it was done two years ago and the contract for another length was let only last fall. It is just for the reason the leader of the opposition has mentioned that that has been done. I suppose everybody appreciates receiving credit for what he gets in his constituency; but if my hon. friend will look up the amount which goes to Shelburne-Yarmouth, he will find that there is a revote from last year of $67,000, money that was not spent, and the other votes are small. I only wish they were bigger. My hon. friend knows that the county of Shelburne-Yarmouth is a shore county going right around the whole nose of Nova Scotia from Port Maitland to Sable River. There are breakwaters and wharves and there is need for many more. These things can be done only gradually, and my hon. friend knows the pressure that is brought to bear in connection with them. I am endeavouring to serve my county as best I can, and I am only sorry I cannot get more.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
In looking over the estimates for the province of New Brunswick I am pleased to note that the county I have the honour to represent is not wholly overlooked. During the past seven sessions I have brought to the attention of the minister the necessity for making the extension to the breakwater at Seal Cove and Woodward's Cove, Grand Manan, and also an extension to the wharf at Beaver Harbour. I am very glad that the minister at last has recognized the great need for these works, and has placed an amount in the estmiates to carry to completion the extension to the breakwater that was started many years ago in the interests of the fishing industry. I am also very glad that there is an amount for the dredging and the breakwater at White Head. I wish to assure the minister that it will be appreciated by the people of that little island out in the bay of Fundy. But I desire to call the attention of the minister to one portion of the island of Grand Manan that has been overlooked and neglected for many years, more particularly since 1921. This is the most exposed place of the island of Grand Manan, which without doubt is in the most exposed position along the whole of the

2294	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.
bay of Fundy. I refer to the village of Cas-taiia. During the election campaign of 1921, and again in 1925 and 1926, it was definitely promised by the Liberal candidates and by those who were working in the interests of the Liberal party, that if this government were returned to power a breakwater would be constructed of the village of Castalia. It is needless for me to tell the minister that the people loyally carried out their program and have been waiting patiently for the government to implement that promise. I wish to say to the minister that no portion of Grand Manan should receive greater consideration at the hands of this administration than the village to which I have referred, in view of the support the people have given them. The village of Castalia was at one time a prosperous fishing community, but like many other places along the coast it has suffered from the tides and winds of the bay of Fundy and from the waves beating on the shore, so that the waterfront and buildings have been destroyed. There is no protection whatever. And in the event of storms the fishermen have to moor their boats two miles from home which entails another hardship. Under such conditions it is impossible to get young men to remain in the place and carry on their vocation. The older men are compelled to stay, but many of the young men have left and gone to the United States where they are following their occupation under more favourable conditions. It is generally believed by the people of Castalia that if some consideration were given them by the government many of these young men who have left would return and take up their occupation, while those who are there at the present time would have some inducement to remain. By the expenditure of a small amount of money we may retain the young men in the fishing industry in Castalia and bring back many of those that have left, and this is surely a proposition which the government ought to take seriously into consideration. In my opinion it is a good immigration policy which should be adopted by the government. A few moments ago the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said that we were anxious to claim credit for anything that was obtained for the county. Let me assure the hon. gentleman that if the government will build this breakwater which was promised the people of Castalia I am prepared to give them all the credit, because it is a necessity and is in the interests of the fishing business.
I regret to see that there is nothing in the supplementary estimates for the island of Campobello or Deer island in Passamaquoddy

bay. The population of each of these islands depends upon the fishing industry and I submit that they should receive as much consideration as other fishing centres. The government have at the present time a report from the engineers in their department who have recommended that a wharf be built below Welchpool on the island of Campobello. One of the government supporters from that district was here a short time ago and interviewed the minister and went home with a favourable impression, and I do hope that when the supplementary estimates come down he will not be disappointed. The wharf at Stewarttown is one that should be provided in the interests of the fishing industry of that place. In these two places, Welchpool and Stewarttown, the people are carrying on the fishing industry just as they did fifty years ago. There are no facilities for them to unload or load their boats and they are bound to follow the old fashioned method of anchoring their boats to keep them afloat and then wading ashore. Now you cannot expect young men to remain in the place if they are obliged to work under such conditions, and I strongly urge the minister, therefore, to bring down in his supplementary estimates provision for the breakwater at Castalia, for the wharf below Welchpool and for the wharf at Stewarttown, all of which are small undertakings. If he does so he will find a more contented people in that fishing centre. The fishermen as a class should receive every consideration at the hands of the government and we should do everything in our power to help the industry. I notice in the reports of the fisheries department that in our county alone last year there was a decrease in the fishing business of $430,000; and taking the whole province of New Brunswick the record is a million dollars less than it was in 1926. It is incumbent upon the government to give this matter the most serious consideration, because fishing is one of the largest industries in the county.
I cannot over-emphasize the fact that if you want to keep young men at work in that industry, if you want to prevent the place from deteriorating at the rate it has done in the last year or two, it is absolutely necessary to carry out these undertakings. I have urged upon the minister building wharves and breakwaters and making extensions wherever necessary. If this is done we shall serve the interests not only of the people of the county but of the province of New Brunswick.
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer, and that is the wharf at Digdeguash basin. That wharf will be greatly appreciated

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.
by the people of that district who have many dealings with the residents of the islands. I wish to impress upon the minister, before I conclude, the importance of keeping in mind the wharves I have mentioned. I trust that when he brings down his supplementary estimates they will contain an amount to cover these various items. He must not lose sight of the importance of the breakwater at Castalia, where nature has formed a splendid foundation of solid rock in the most suitable place along the shore. All that is necessary now is for the government to carry the work to completion. If they will do so they will implement the promises they made in 1921 and 1926 and it will mean a great deal to the fishing industry of that locality.

Lomeville is a very prosperous village of fishermen. It is an important fishing centre; it has valuable salmon and lobster fisheries. Last year the minister almost accomplished something, a thing which his predecessors had failed to do, although urged repeatedly to meet the necessities of the case. He put in sufficient vote to do the work, but it has been imperfectly and unsatisfactorily carried out. I believe there was something like $15,000 voted for dredging and' if that amount had been expended I think it would have been sufficient to accomplish the desired results.
